climate-energy-9cf7dcf00d.headline: COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya
climate-energy-9cf7dcf00d.fulltext:
COP31: Key outcomes agreed at the UN climate talks in Antalya
The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, have failed to reach agreement on a “pact” that lacked clear references to curbing fossil fuels or scaling up climate finance.
The “Antalya pact”, proposed by the joint Turkish-Australian presidency, was rejected in the final hours by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable nations.
Meanwhile, many developing countries criticised the lack of progress on climate finance and indecision on a proposed $120bn target for funding climate adaptation.
With stark divisions preventing agreement on the presidency-led pact, UNFCCC chief Simon Stiell expressed “deep disappointment”, speaking of “scope to improve, modernise and reform” the UN climate process.
Despite a chaotic endgame that saw the overrunning COP become the longest in history, it did not end in complete failure, with many items adopted in the closing plenary.
These included fairly limited or procedural outcomes on a new “mechanism” for global “just transitions”, plus support for countries struck by climate disasters.
There was some progress beyond the negotiations, though, with growing coalitions of nations championing “roadmaps” for “transitioning away” from fossil fuels.
With the presidency promoting “electrification” as a key theme, around 80 nations also signed up to a global target of securing 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035.
Here, Carbon Brief provides in-depth analysis of all the key outcomes from Antalya, both inside and outside the COP31 negotiations.
(See Carbon Brief’s coverage of COP30, COP29, COP28, COP27, COP26, COP25, COP24, COP23, COP22, COP21 and COP20.)
Formal negotiations
Turkish and Australian leadership
Turkey and Australia presided over the longest COP in history – and failed to find consensus on their proposed “cover decision”, exposing deep fractures between countries on key issues such as fossil fuels and the need for developed nations to meet climate-finance pledges.
Experts told Carbon Brief that, strictly, the talks did not “collapse” as several negotiated items were still adopted.
Rather, the rejection of the cover decision represented, for the first time, “those who want a higher level of ambition actively reject[ing] the lowest common denominator on offer”, said one veteran observer.
Dispute over who would host COP31 – representing the “western Europe and other states” region – had gone on for three years.
In the end, the two main rivals, Turkey and Australia, agreed to a deal last year at COP30 that the summit would take place in Antalya, Turkey, with Australia acting as “president of negotiations”.
Critics questioned whether either country was well-placed to host, given their ongoing fossil-fuel expansion.
Turkey faced criticism for announcing the discovery of two new oil fields on the eve of the summit, while recent Carbon Brief analysis found that Australia is the third-largest CO2 exporter in history because of its fossil-fuel production.
Ahead of the summit, the presidency released four official letters outlining a vision for COP31.
The first letter, written by COP31 president Murat Kurum in April 2026, confirmed the appointment of Australian climate minister Chris Bowen as “president of the negotiations” and announced that a pre-COP would be held in Fiji in October.
The second letter, authored by both Kurum and Bowen from the Copenhagen climate ministerial in May, said that “COP31 presents a vital opportunity to further accelerate…in the areas of clean energy, electrification and resilient infrastructure”.
The third letter, published in August 2026, gave more details on the presidency’s plans for the “action agenda” – the part of the UN process that mobilises coalitions of nations and non-state actors to push climate action further.
This letter also introduced a key aim from the presidency to get countries to agree to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to 35% by 2035 (often referred to as “35 by 35”). (See: Electrification.)
The final letter, published in October ahead of the pre-COP in Fiji, said that the presidency would centre on “delivering a COP focused on accelerating implementation, electrification and resilience in an uncertain world”.
It added that “many parties have emphasised the importance of reviewing and continuously improving UNFCCC processes, to ensure it remains fit for purpose, sustainable and focused as negotiations evolve over time”, adding:
“At COP31, we will hold presidency consultations to hear parties’ views on how to strengthen UNFCCC processes, to ensure growing demands are met and to effectively deploy resources.”
The pre-COP in Fiji was held from 5-8 October and was attended by 3,000 people.
In this somewhat intimate setting, Bowen announced that Turkey and Australia had agreed to negotiate a “presidency-led” cover decision at COP31.
He added that revealing this before COP was part of the presidency’s “upfront, transparent and consultative approach”.
Later that month, the presidency named the five ministerial pairs from developed and developing countries that would take key negotiation issues forward at COP31. These issues were mitigation, adaptation, finance, just transition and oceans.
COP31 kicked off on 9 November, with climate negotiations scholar (and Carbon Brief contributing editor) Dr Joanna Depledge noting that it was clear from the summit’s opening ceremony that “Australia [was] the junior partner” in the presidency.
COP’s opening day ran late into the night as the presidency worked to avert a fight over proposed changes to the summit’s negotiations agenda.
    
        
         
                Agenda adopted! Moments ago in Antalya, Turkey, COP31 president Murat Kurum outlined how an “agenda fight” has been averted, despite various proposals for additions to proceedings. This came after a short delay, while a series of huddles took place on…            
            
                COP31: Agenda adopted!            
        
The next day, in plenary, Kurum announced that a resolution had been found.
He said that calls for new agenda items on adaptation finance and trade were rejected, whereas an item on a new climate finance “work programme” had been added. (The EU expressed “deep concern” about the addition.)
Kurum added that two extra proposed items on mountains and climate change – made more poignant by recent catastrophic floods in Nepal – were also not added to the agenda. However, he said that the presidency would instead hold consultations on the topic.
Though an early scrap over the agenda was avoided, the summit’s opening days were plagued with logistical problems.
Attendees were forced to spend hours navigating traffic and queues just to get into the venue – sparking serious access concerns.
The problems persisted into the first day of the world leaders’ summit on 11 November, when delegates were informed that they should travel between the hours of 5-7am to secure access to the venue. Ire only grew when security staff still let people in after this time.
On Friday morning, the presidency released a “reflections” text from its consultations with countries on what they would like to see in a cover decision. This was an “informal note” with a bullet-pointed list of topics that might be included.
On Saturday evening, Kurum told a press conference that “around 30 countries” had indicated support for the 35 by 35 pledge.
However, he had little to share on progress in the negotiations and eluded questions on how he planned to include “fossil fuels” in the cover decision.
In the small hours of Sunday morning, half-way through the summit, Kurum announced presidency and ministerial consultations on “outstanding political issues”.
He also invited ministers to a “divan” – a group meeting, not a daybed – to discuss cross-cutting issues.
On Monday afternoon, the presidency dropped an 18-page first draft of its proposed cover decision – along with a short “presidency note” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text. (See: Cover decision.)
At a press conference, Bowen told journalists that the presidency decided to release the text “early” to allow parties to debate on it for as long as possible and acknowledged that it would need to be “refined” down.
On Wednesday evening, the presidency held its divan, where delegation heads sat in a circle and were asked to share their priorities for finding consensus in the negotiations.
Speaking at the divan, Kurum told parties that the second draft cover decision would be published that evening.
In the end, the second draft cover decision was published on Thursday.
Later that day, Kurum and Bowen spoke at a press conference, talking up their latest draft with lofty claims that it could “achieve [the] covenant of 1.5C and nothing more”.
However, the second draft was rejected by countries and civil society alike. (See: Cover decision.)
On Friday – the summit’s last scheduled day – the mood at COP soured. With few official updates, delegates relied on ever-changing rumours about when a new text might emerge.
Negotiations on other key issues also remained stuck, as civil society dubbed it the “worst COP in history” at a press conference attended by Carbon Brief.
In the evening, the presidency opened the closing plenary to gavel through non-contentious items – and announced that a new text would not be released until Saturday morning.
They were interrupted by a protester wearing a shirt that said “you are killing the future” and with a red noose around their neck.
As talks ran into overtime on Saturday, any kind of official update failed to arrive.
An open letter signed by 100 civil society organisations told the presidency it was “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs the UNFCCC has ever had”.
As Turkish support staff started packing down the party pavilions, behind-the-scenes disputes between country ministers intensified.
Carbon Brief understands that 126 countries – made up of the EU, UK, the Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), the Independent Association of Latin America and the Caribbean (AILAC), the Umbrella Group (UG) and least-developed countries (LDCs) – approached the presidency as a united front to demand changes to the cover decision.
These changes included on how it referenced transitioning away from fossil fuels, adaptation finance and carbon capture and storage. (See: Cover decision.)
A new draft cover decision did not arrive until the early hours of Sunday morning.
With official updates still few and far between, rumours swirled that many countries were still not happy with this iteration of the text and planned to reject it.
Later that day, another version of the text arrived – but it contained only minor changes.
In a fiery final plenary session on Sunday afternoon, several countries rejected the cover decision – citing reasons including its failure to respond to humanity’s overshoot of 1.5C of global warming, its failure to clearly mention fossil fuels and its lack of clear figures for adaptation finance. (See: Cover decision.)
While countries rejected the cover decision, they did find consensus on other texts, including for the just transition work programme, the global goal on adaptation, the climate finance work programme, carbon markets, long-term finance and “Article 2.1c”.
The final gavel came down at 7:33pm local time – nearly 50 hours after the summit’s scheduled end. This makes COP31 the longest in history.

The final draft of a COP31 “cover decision” was rejected by at least 32 counties during a chaotic – and, at times, acrimonious – closing plenary in Antalya.

india-9c9ef26be5.headline: 'A Pact For Growth, Jobs': India, EU Likely To Sign Trade Deal In December
india-9c9ef26be5.fulltext:
The EU Ambassador to India said the signed agreement will be reviewed by the European Parliament, which will have final say before the FTA can enter into force.
The India-EU bilateral trade in goods stood at EUR 118 billion in 2025.
The India-European Union Free Trade Agreement (FTA) is likely to be signed in December and could take effect by mid-2027, European Union (EU) Ambassador to India Jean-Eric Paquet said in a detailed video message giving a timeline of the entire process. He said the negotiation between the two sides concluded successfully in January this year and the teams are now working on technical refining.
"An agreement that will make a difference for growth and jobs on both sides." - @EUAmbIndia explains the timeline and the road ahead. Where does the FTA stand, and what comes next? This is the first in our series on what the FTA will deliver. Stay tuned for more updates," the X post with the video message read.
The India-EU bilateral trade in goods stood at EUR 118 billion in 2025, according to the European Commission and this trade relation is expected to take a boost after the agreement comes into force.
Ambassador Paquet said the European Commission sent a proposal to the Council in September for signing of the agreement and European ministers would give the final go-ahead for its signing.
The EU Ambassador to India gave an idea of the next steps following the signing of the deal. He said the agreement, once signed, will be reviewed thoroughly by the European Parliament, which will have final say before the FTA can enter into force.
Noting that European Parliament's Foreign Affairs Committee had recently visited Delhi, Paquet said the chair of the Committee is expecting the Parliament to form its decision in coming months, expressing optimism about a positive outcome.
"Once the free trade agreement is signed, on the European side, we then move to the scrutiny of the European Parliament, which needs to give its assent. We just had the Foreign Affairs Committee of the European Parliament in Delhi, and they explained how this works. There will be substantial scrutiny of the document, but then the European Parliament can only say whether it agrees with the agreement or not, so it doesn't open a new negotiation," he said.
"The chair of the committee said that he expects the Parliament to form a view in spring, and he was very, very optimistic that it would be a positive view. So, I'm not saying it on behalf of the European Parliament; I'm quoting the chair of the Foreign Affairs Committee in the European Parliament. With that, the free trade agreement can then enter into force, let's say by the middle of 2027. And this means that at entry into force, the benefits occur," he added.
The much-awaited India-EU Free Trade Agreement is aimed at benefiting labour-intensive sectors, including textiles, apparel, leather, footwear, marine products, gems and jewellery, handicrafts, engineering goods and automobiles. Once enforced, it will reduce the tariffs on nearly USD 33 billion worth of Indian exports in labour-intensive sectors to zero.
However, India has taken steps to safeguard sensitive sectors, including dairy, cereals, poultry and certain other agricultural products. The pact also covers services, digital trade, customs and trade facilitation, intellectual property rights and mobility of professionals.
The deal goes beyond products and services, bringing a way and method for skilled Indian professionals to go to European countries. This covers intra-corporate transferees, contractual service suppliers and independent professionals across several sectors.

science-mind-fb4dab8b86.headline: Air Pollution Reprograms Brain Immune Cells, Raises Dementia Risk by 25%
science-mind-fb4dab8b86.fulltext:
Summary:
A new study reveals that fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) raises dementia risk by 25% and triggers Alzheimer’s-like brain damage even without amyloid plaques. The research shows that inhaled pollution reprograms the brain’s resident immune cells (microglia), compromises the blood-brain barrier, drains cellular energy reserves, and kills newborn neurons in the hippocampus.
Key Facts:
- 25% Higher Dementia Risk: Analyzing nearly 500,000 adults in the UK Biobank over up to 14 years, researchers found that individuals living in the most polluted areas faced a 25% greater risk of developing Alzheimer’s or related dementias, independent of age, smoking, diabetes, or inherited genetic risk.
- Microglial Reprogramming & Barrier Breakdown: Mice exposed to concentrated outdoor fine particulate matter (PM2.5) for five months developed a leaky blood-brain barrier, chronic neuroinflammation, depleted NAD+/NADH cellular energy ratios, and increased death of newborn hippocampal neurons.
- Damage Even Without Amyloid Plaques: Air pollution disrupted gene expression in microglia and caused memory deficits in healthy mice entirely lacking amyloid plaques, while accelerating plaque buildup in Alzheimer’s-prone models.
Source: Case Western Reserve University
Microscopic soot, industrial emissions, and wildfire smoke, collectively categorized as fine particulate matter 2.5 (PM2.5), have long been recognized as major drivers of cardiovascular and respiratory disease. Mounting epidemiological evidence has also linked polluted air to cognitive decline, yet whether inhaled particles actively cause dementia, and precisely how they injure the brain, has remained an urgent scientific question.
Now, a comprehensive translational study published in the Journal of Neuroinflammation by researchers at Case Western Reserve University, University Hospitals, and the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center provides compelling human and experimental evidence that air pollution directly fuels neurodegeneration by hijacking the brain’s immune system.
Led by co-senior authors Dr. Sanjay Rajagopalan and Dr. Andrew Pieper, the research team combined population-scale human health tracking with controlled five-month inhalation experiments in mice to map the cellular chain reaction linking dirty air to dementia.
Half a Million Human Records Show a 25% Risk Surge
To quantify how long-term air pollution exposure shapes dementia risk across diverse genetic backgrounds, the researchers analyzed medical and environmental records from roughly 500,000 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank, tracked for up to 14 years.
Even after controlling for confounding variables, including age, smoking status, diabetes, and socioeconomic factors—people residing in the most polluted third of geographic regions were 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease or a related dementia than those living in the cleanest third. Crucially, high air pollution elevated dementia risk regardless of whether an individual carried high or low inherited genetic risk for Alzheimer’s.
Recreating City Pollution Reveals Immune Reprogramming
To test causation directly, the investigators exposed mice to real-world outdoor Cleveland air for five months, concentrating PM2.5 particles to match levels recorded in the world’s most heavily polluted urban centers.
Even in otherwise healthy mice without genetic predispositions to neurodegeneration, chronic PM2.5 exposure triggered widespread brain pathology:
- Microglial Dysfunction: Pollution fundamentally altered which genes were switched on and off inside microglia—the brain’s resident immune cells responsible for clearing cellular debris and fighting infection—pushing them into a disrupted, inflammatory state.
- Leaky Blood-Brain Barrier: Treated mice developed structural breakdown of the protective blood-brain barrier alongside sustained neuroinflammation.
- Energy Collapse and Neuron Death: Polluted brains exhibited a sharp drop in the NAD+/NADH ratio, a critical metabolic indicator of cellular energy resilience, accompanied by accelerated death of newly born neurons in the hippocampus, the brain’s primary hub for learning and memory.
Remarkably, these memory deficits and Alzheimer’s-like cellular injuries emerged in healthy mice completely devoid of amyloid plaques. When the researchers exposed mice genetically engineered to develop Alzheimer’s pathology to the same polluted air, the particles inflicted identical neuroinflammatory and metabolic damage while simultaneously accelerating amyloid plaque accumulation.
Protecting Brain Resilience Against Environmental Stress
“By recreating in mice what happens when people breathe polluted air, we found that pollution causes major changes in which genes are active in the brain’s immune cells,” explained Rajagopalan, professor of medicine and director of the Cardiovascular Research Institute at Case Western Reserve School of Medicine. “These cells normally keep the brain healthy by clearing away debris and fighting infection. Seeing how pollution disrupts them helps explain how a stress that affects much of the world’s population harms the brain, and it points us toward a way to treat it.”
“We’ve identified a key way that air pollution harms the healthy brain and speeds up Alzheimer’s disease,” added Pieper, director of the Harrington Discovery Institute Brain Health Medicines Center and psychiatrist at the Louis Stokes Cleveland VA Medical Center. “This helps us understand how factors in our environment can accelerate and intensify brain diseases of aging. It also opens the door to studying other environmental stresses on the brain, and to finding ways to keep the brain resilient even when we can’t avoid those stressors.”
Questions and Answers
How much does air pollution increase the risk of developing dementia?
In an analysis of nearly 500,000 adults tracked for up to 14 years, researchers found that people living in areas with the highest levels of fine particulate air pollution were 25% more likely to develop Alzheimer’s disease or related dementias than those in the cleanest areas, even among people with low genetic risk.
What does fine particulate air pollution (PM2.5) physically do to the brain?
In mouse experiments recreating urban air pollution, inhaled PM2.5 particles caused the blood-brain barrier to leak, triggered brain inflammation, lowered cellular energy reserves (NAD+/NADH ratio), killed newborn memory neurons in the hippocampus, and reprogrammed the genes of the brain’s immune cells (microglia).
Does air pollution only harm brains that already have Alzheimer’s plaques?
No. Researchers were struck to find that air pollution caused memory problems, immune cell disruption, and neuron death in healthy mice that had no amyloid plaques at all, while also speeding up plaque buildup in mice genetically prone to Alzheimer’s disease.

- This article was edited by a Neuroscience News editor.
- Journal paper reviewed in full.
- Additional context added by our staff.

Pieper & Sanjay Rajagopalan.
- DOI: 10.1186/s12974-026-04118-1
Abstract
Air pollution exposure interacts with Alzheimer’s genetic susceptibility to reshape microglial epigenomic and transcriptional programs
Chronic exposure to fine particulate matter air pollution (PM2.5) is associated with cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease, but the biology connecting inhaled particles to the brain remains incompletely defined. Among 475,325 eligible UK Biobank participants, long-term PM2.5 exposure and Alzheimer disease (AD) polygenic risk were both independently associated with higher risk of AD and related dementias (ADRD).
The PM2.5-by-polygenic risk score (PRS) interaction in Cox models was statistically significant but sub-multiplicative or below unity (interaction HR 0.981, 95% CI 0.965–0.998; p = 0.026), indicating that the combined association was smaller than the simple product of the two individual associations.
To define the underlying biology, we exposed 5xFAD mice, an amyloid-based model of AD, and wild-type (WT) littermates to concentrated ambient PM2.5 or filtered air for 20 weeks. PM2.5 exposure activated microglia, disrupted the blood-brain barrier, depleted the brain NAD+/NADH pool required for resilience and repair, impaired postnatal hippocampal neurogenesis, and caused cognitive deficits.
In 5xFAD mice it additionally increased amyloid burden. Paired RNA-seq and ATAC-seq of microglia isolated from the same animals showed that exposure remodeled both gene expression and chromatin accessibility, and that that magnitude and direction of this response depended on genotype, converging on inflammatory, lysosomal, oxidative-stress, synaptic, and amyloid-related pathways.
These population-scale data in humans and experimental data in mice support PM2.5 as an environmental neurotoxicant and define microglial regulatory programs through which genetic background shapes the biological response to a common and modifiable exposure.

beyond-your-beat-30e263cbe2.headline: India pledges $1.6bn in flood relief for Nepal as Balendra Shah visits Modi
beyond-your-beat-30e263cbe2.fulltext:
India pledges $1.6bn in flood relief for Nepal as Balendra Shah visits Modi
Nepal’s PM Balendra Shah is in New Delhi for a two-day visit – his first since coming to power in March.
India will provide Nepal with a $1.62bn economic package in the wake of August’s devastating floods in the country, which led to the deaths and disappearances of thousands of people.
The sum announced on Monday is one of its largest-ever relief commitments, and comes as New Delhi boosts ties with its Himalayan neighbour, where it competes with China for influence.
The announcement followed talks between India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Nepali counterpart Balendra Shah, who is in New Delhi for a two-day visit – his first bilateral trip abroad since coming to power in March.
“We express our deep condolences for the loss of lives caused by the devastating floods in Nepal in August,” Modi said, standing alongside Shah in New Delhi. “To support Nepal’s reconstruction, and give fresh momentum to its long-term development, we announce a development cooperation package worth 240 billion Nepali rupees [$1.6bn].”
August’s floods, which scientists say were caused by the effects of climate change, were triggered when part of a mountain glacier collapsed and a torrent of water and mud flooded down into Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot regions, as well as into China’s Tibet region on August 26. More than 1,300 people have been confirmed dead, and more than 5,000 remain missing.
In October, the United Nations’ climate loss and damage fund set aside a sum of $20m for aid to Nepal.
India’s package will include a $377m grant for post-disaster reconstruction and new infrastructure projects, and a $1.24bn line of credit for energy projects, the countries said in a joint statement.
India is Nepal’s largest trading partner, accounting for more than 60 percent of its imports, worth $8.6bn, while China accounts for 13 percent, or $1.8bn, according to World Bank figures.
Besides the flood relief package, the pair agreed on further cooperation in education and research, satellite communications, and sustainable urban development. The two leaders also jointly opened a train link connecting the countries.
“May the friendship between Nepal and India be one where trust stands as tall as the Himalayas,” said Shah.

ai-27065c561f.headline: Anthropic launches Claude Ship, letting AI agents review, fix, and approve code changes
ai-27065c561f.fulltext:
Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. On Monday, the newly public AI company announced the launch of Claude Ship, a suite of AI agents for automating code reviews, fixes, and approvals of routine code changes.
The latter is the more interesting part of this new set of tools, as AI coding tools already offered code review features before now. What’s notable about Claude Ship is not just that it can review proposed code changes and identify and address problems, but that it also includes an agent that can approve code changes automatically based on policies set by a development team.
The launch arrives at a time when AI coding agents have become increasingly capable of generating substantial amounts of code, leading to bottlenecks in reviewing and approving the code changes before they go live. With Claude Ship, the idea is to automate even more of the work involved in the development process, essentially by delegating approval authority to an AI agent itself.
“Most teams want a person to approve every change, and that’s easy to keep up with when people write every line. But a lot of developers build with agents now,” a company blog post explains. “On the Claude Code team, Claude writes most of our code, and we wanted everything after the PR to move that fast too.”
Claude Ship is launching in beta, allowing early adopters to use it to review pull requests (PRs), and then decide what’s ready to merge.
The new offering consists of Code Review, which is already generally available, and two new agents now in beta: PR Steward and Claude Approvals. PR Steward focuses on addressing issues such as failing CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback from Code Review. It also comments after every push on what it changed and how to roll it back, if needed.
Claude Approvals then applies an approval policy that the team writes as a file in the repository. This approval process can incorporate various signals, including Code Review findings or the company’s own classifiers, with policies written in natural language.
Because the offering is still in beta, Anthropic suggests running the approval functionality in observe-only mode first. Teams can also choose to start with just one repository and set monthly spending limits to have more control over the process.
Anthropic says teams will also still remain in control of where Claude Ship runs, which review settings to use (e.g., Quick, Standard, or Deep), and which changes should be escalated to a human for a decision.
Claude Ship is rolling out to Claude Team and Enterprise plans for repositories on GitHub. Code Review is generally available, while PR Steward and Claude Approvals are in beta.

ai-6a7990e1ad.headline: Amazon snaps up Decart’s AI optimization tech for $7.5B as it prepares to sell Trainium chips
ai-6a7990e1ad.fulltext:
Amazon has agreed to acquire a good chunk of Israeli startup Decart.
The e-commerce and cloud giant is paying $7.5 billion for the startup, according to Bloomberg.
Decart has made a name for itself building interactive real-time world models — most recently Oasis 3 — and AI video-generation tools. But under the hood, the company stands out for its Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), software that helps AI models run efficiently on Nvidia, Amazon, and Google’s hardware.
As part of the deal, Amazon will acquire the technology behind DOS, as well as Decart’s founding team and team of AI researchers and engineers, Amazon said in a blog post.
“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, quantum computing, at Amazon. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.”
Amazon, which has so far been using its Trainium chips at its own data centers, is preparing to start selling them to customers as a competitor to Nvidia. Decart’s technology could make it easier for customers to run their workloads on Amazon chips, rather than Nvidia’s, which has been the gold standard so far.
Decart and Amazon did not immediately return requests for comment.

Chinese military researchers fear that AI advances could give the US an edge in the nuclear balance of power. Experts in China worry that artificial intelligence could make it easier for US forces to detect and destroy Chinese nuclear missiles, according to a New York Times analysis. That would undermine China's deterrence strategy, which relies on a guaranteed second-strike capability.
Researchers at the Academy of Military Sciences in Beijing write that AI could shrink US decision-making time from 15 to 30 minutes down to 90 seconds. China currently has about 620 operational warheads, according to the Federation of American Scientists, and is expected to expand its arsenal to roughly 1,000 by 2030. At the same time, Chinese military institutes are studying how AI could make their own weapons harder to intercept, for instance by using AI-controlled flight paths for hypersonic missiles.
Experts warn, however, that flawed AI data could trigger dangerous miscalculations during a crisis. That risk proved very real earlier this year, when the US military nearly boarded a Chinese ship based on a false, AI-generated intelligence report. Xi Jinping did discuss nuclear risks at a summit with Trump and Putin, but AI's role in nuclear weapons never came up, according to the report. India AI funding nearly doubles to $1.6B in Jan-Sept 2026: Tracxn
Early-stage funding led the investment mix. Mumbai overtook Bengaluru to become the city with the largest funding during the period.
India AI companies raised $1.6 billion in equity funding in the first nine months of 2026, nearly double the level in the year-ago period, according to a report by Tracxn Technologies.
This, in fact, is the highest funding grosser across the nine-month periods covered since 2019.
"India AI companies raised $1.6 billion in equity funding in nine months 2026, up 96% from $822 million in nine months 2025 and 162% from $616 million in nine months 2024, marking the highest funding total across the nine-month periods covered since 2019," the report by data intelligence platform Tracxn Technologies' said.
According to the 'India AI - 9M 2026' report, the funding was raised across 87 rounds, compared to 149 rounds during the year-ago period. This indicates that the increase was driven by a relatively small number of large deals.
Early-stage funding led the investment mix. Mumbai overtook Bengaluru to become the city with the largest funding during the period.
The ten largest rounds in 2026 raised $1.5 billion, 90% of the $1.6 billion total.
Neysa, a Mumbai-based AI cloud provider, raised the largest chunk, a $600 million Series B in February, equivalent to 37% of all funding. Sarvam, the Bengaluru-based generative AI developer, raised $255 million in a Series B in June and a further $90.4 million in August. Yotta raised $150 million in July.
"Series A and later rounds fell 33% to 24 from 36, and first-time funded companies fell 60% to 24 from 60," the report said.
Globally, AI companies raised $383.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026; India's $1.6 billion was 0.4% of that, ninth among countries.
Early-stage funding rose 191% to $1.3 billion between January and September, up from $434 million in the year-ago period. Early-stage rounds fell 38% to 21. The average early-stage round was $60.2 million against $12.8 million in the year-ago period.
According to the report, 111 investors backed India AI companies in the first nine months of 2026, down from 169 in the year-ago period. First-time investors fell to 43, and international investors fell to 29.
Peak XV Partners led early-stage investors with three investments, followed by Prosus and Khosla Ventures with two each. Antler, IvyCap Ventures and Finvolve made two seed investments each, while SoftBank Vision Fund and Creaegis backed one late-stage round each.

The US Department of Commerce has added Megaspeed, the Singapore-based cloud computing firm at the centre of the ongoing Nvidia saga, to its trade blacklist, hours after the chip giant reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO following his abrupt departure 11 days prior.
In a filing released on Monday, the department’s Bureau of Industry and Security placed Megaspeed International and six other entities in Southeast Asia – widely regarded as Megaspeed’s affiliates – on its Entity List. The agency cited “the significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorised end uses or end users”.
Effective immediately ahead of formal publication on Wednesday, the move blocks suppliers from shipping US-regulated technology to the blacklisted firms without first acquiring a special licence, which Washington would likely reject. Goods already in transit have a 30-day grace period.
Alongside Megaspeed International Pte Ltd – also listed under aliases including 7Road International – the blacklist targets entities across Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand: Swiftdata, Apex Enterprise Solutions, Speedmatrix, MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International and Megaspeed (Thailand).
In a statement to the South China Morning Post last week, the company said it “conducts legitimate and lawful business” and that it had hired outside lawyers to carry out an internal investigation. It added that former executive Alice Huang left the firm in August 2025.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Tuesday.
The addition to the Entity List came on the same day Nvidia announced it reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO and board director. The chipmaker said it made the decision after receiving backing from US President Donald Trump and assurances from senior US officials that Huang’s return posed no national security risk.
Huang had resigned on November 12 after acknowledging extramarital affairs, triggering a sell-off across Nvidia and broader US tech stocks. Shares in the chipmaker surged more than 30 per cent on Monday following news of his return.
He reportedly had an affair with Alice Huang, who is suspected of acting as a Chinese spy – an allegation Beijing has firmly denied.
Washington’s trade restrictions also followed an announcement days earlier that the US Commerce and Justice departments were conducting a joint investigation into Megaspeed for potential criminal conduct.
According to the two agencies, the Commerce Department opened its inquiry in 2024 after detecting suspicious activity while monitoring for the diversion of sensitive semiconductors. The Justice Department is leading a parallel criminal investigation into possible violations of US chip export controls.
Investigators requested records from Nvidia in May 2025 regarding direct or indirect sales to Megaspeed, prompting the chipmaker to place the firm on its internal “no-sell” list the following month, the departments said.
Ann Cao is a Shanghai-based technology reporter for the Post, covering technology start-ups and policies in the city and eastern China. She graduated from the University of Hong Kong with a master's degree in journalism.

deep-tech-8a4cf592a5.headline: IBM quantum computer solves problem classical computers can’t in just 15 minutes
deep-tech-8a4cf592a5.fulltext:
IBM quantum computer solves problem classical computers can’t in just 15 minutes
- Date:
  November 23, 2026
- Source:
  IBM
- Summary:
  IBM and University of Chicago researchers have demonstrated that a quantum computer can complete an extraordinarily complex calculation in just 15 minutes, beyond the practical reach of leading classical computing methods. A novel error-detection technique also allows scientists to establish confidence in the accuracy of the results, overcoming a major hurdle in quantum computing.
- Share:
An IBM quantum computer has completed an extraordinarily complex computational task in just 15 minutes, while leading methods for simulating the calculation on conventional computers would require prohibitively long runtimes. Perhaps even more significantly, researchers were able to establish statistical confidence in the accuracy of the quantum computer's results, addressing one of the biggest obstacles in the field.
The achievement, led by IBM and researchers from the University of Chicago, satisfies the fundamental criteria for quantum advantage. This milestone occurs when a quantum computer performs a computational task beyond the practical capabilities of leading classical computing methods while producing results that can be trusted.
In their new paper, "Sampling hard circuits with verifiably high fidelity," the researchers demonstrated that both objectives could be achieved simultaneously using a novel design for encoded quantum circuits. The experiment represents one of the largest demonstrations of logical quantum computing to date. The researchers have also made their circuits and experimental results publicly available through the Quantum Advantage Tracker.
Solving Quantum Computing's Verification Problem
Unlike conventional computers, which process information using bits that represent either zero or one, quantum computers rely on quantum bits, or qubits. These can exist in combinations of both states and interact through a phenomenon known as quantum entanglement. These properties allow quantum computers to approach certain computational problems in fundamentally different ways.
For years, scientists have tested the capabilities of quantum computers using a benchmark called random circuit sampling (RCS). This technique involves running a series of randomly selected quantum operations and generating samples from a complex probability distribution. As the circuits grow larger and more complicated, reproducing their output with a classical computer becomes increasingly difficult.
However, this approach creates a fundamental dilemma. If a computation is too difficult for a classical computer to reproduce, how can researchers establish that the quantum computer performed it correctly?
As computational complexity increases, independently verifying the results becomes progressively more difficult and eventually impractical without making strong assumptions about how accurately the quantum hardware operates.
To overcome this problem, the IBM and University of Chicago team developed a more structured alternative to random circuit sampling. The researchers mathematically demonstrated that their approach preserves the same computational hardness criteria as conventional RCS while introducing a structure that allows errors to be detected during the computation.
"Verification remains one of the biggest challenges in firmly establishing experimental quantum advantage," said Bill Fefferman, Associate Professor at the University of Chicago. "This experiment develops techniques to better characterize the fidelity of hard quantum states under noise, increasing confidence that the quantum computer is solving a computationally hard problem."
Soumik Ghosh, PhD student in Fefferman's group at the University of Chicago, added, "Beyond strengthening experimental validation, advances in verification have the potential to unlock practical applications for the next generation of quantum computers."
70 Logical Qubits and Tenfold Lower Error Rates
One of the greatest challenges in building powerful quantum computers is their extraordinary sensitivity to errors. Quantum information can be disrupted by environmental disturbances, imperfections in hardware, and inaccuracies in the operations used to manipulate qubits. As computations become longer and more complex, these errors can accumulate and undermine the reliability of the results.
Quantum error correction addresses this weakness by encoding quantum information across multiple physical qubits to create more reliable units known as logical qubits. This approach allows certain errors to be identified and, depending on the technique, corrected or accounted for without destroying the underlying quantum information.
In one of the largest known demonstrations of quantum error correction, the researchers performed computations using 70 protected logical qubits. The experiment involved 2,415 logical two-qubit operations and 468 logical "T gates."
Quantum gates are the fundamental operations that manipulate quantum information, much like logic gates in conventional computers. Two-qubit gates allow qubits to interact, while T gates enable additional types of quantum operations needed for universal quantum computing. Together, these gate counts illustrate the considerable complexity of the experiment.
By encoding the quantum circuits, the researchers achieved effective logical error rates 10 times lower than the underlying physical error rates. This substantial reduction allowed the quantum computer to maintain remarkably high fidelity, a measure of how closely the actual quantum state matches the intended one, despite performing thousands of complex operations.
A New Era of Quantum Advantage
"We are now firmly in the quantum advantage era," said Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow. "We have demonstrated a quantum computation beyond the practical reach of classical computers that establishes, with statistical confidence, a lower bound on how faithfully it was executed. This milestone gives scientists, developers, and businesses a new foundation for trusting quantum computers as they scale to problems far beyond what we can achieve classically."
The researchers found that many leading classical simulation techniques would require impractically long periods to reproduce the computation. IBM's quantum computer, by comparison, accomplished the task in approximately 15 minutes.
Although the experiment was designed to demonstrate quantum advantage rather than solve an immediate real-world problem, it addresses two essential requirements for making large-scale quantum computing practical: controlling errors and establishing confidence in computational results.
By demonstrating both capabilities in a computation beyond the practical reach of leading classical methods, the researchers have taken a significant step toward a future in which quantum computers could reliably tackle scientific and industrial problems that are currently out of reach.

deep-tech-de8ec45855.headline: China's humanoid robot stocks draw over 10 billion yuan in a single day as four-ministry policy lands and mass production accelerates
deep-tech-de8ec45855.fulltext:
On Nov. 23, China's National Development and Reform Commission and three other government departments issued an implementation plan for building a service system for the elderly and children, encouraging the development of service robots, exoskeletons and other products for elderly-care scenarios. The same day, five humanoid robot standards issued by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology entered the implementation phase. The policy and liquidity tailwinds, combined with Elon Musk's timetable for Optimus to perform household chores, sent China's A-share humanoid robot sector up nearly 6% on the day, with net inflows of main funds exceeding 10.2 billion yuan (approximately $1.5 billion). Unitree Robotics hit the 20% daily limit, with its market value recovering to 286.361 billion yuan (approximately $43.0 billion), a rebound of about 75% in six weeks. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley had already raised their shipment forecasts, and orders and institutional research visits to supply-chain companies are picking up in tandem, though exchange filings show domestic and foreign funds moving in opposite directions on the limit-up board.
The humanoid robot sector drew concentrated catalysts from policy, industry and capital on Nov. 23. That day, China's National Development and Reform Commission, Ministry of Civil Affairs, National Health Commission and Ministry of Education jointly issued an implementation plan for building a service system for the elderly and children, explicitly encouraging the development of AI agents, service robots, smart wearable devices, exoskeletons and other new products suited to elderly-care scenarios, and supporting the setup of experience zones in nursing homes and communities. Driven by this, China's A-share humanoid robot sector rallied across the board, with the sector index gaining nearly 6% on the day and net inflows of main funds exceeding 10.2 billion yuan (approximately $1.5 billion).
The policy signal went beyond a single document. The same day, five humanoid robot standards previously issued by China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology formally entered the implementation phase, covering three areas — intelligent capability evaluation, key components and training — providing a technical benchmark for the industry's shift from prototype development to volume delivery. On the liquidity front, the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing stock exchanges announced on the evening of Nov. 22 that the minimum margin ratio for margin financing would be lowered from 100% to 80%, with a market-maker system for the ChiNext board also put out for comment, and the Shanghai and Shenzhen exchanges' annual fee cuts adding about 2.758 billion yuan (approximately $413.9 million) in total savings. Some estimates suggest the margin ratio cut alone could theoretically free up nearly 400 billion yuan (approximately $60.0 billion) in incremental capital, and the high-beta robotics sector became one of the preferred destinations for those funds.
At the individual stock level, Unitree Robotics (688836.SS) was the day's most closely watched name. The stock sealed its 20% limit-up around 13:45 in the afternoon, closing at 708 yuan per share, with total market value recovering to 286.361 billion yuan (approximately $43.0 billion), full-day turnover of 4.677 billion yuan (approximately $701.9 million), a turnover rate of 23.99%, and net inflows of main funds of 582 million yuan (approximately $87.3 million). This was the company's second 20% limit-up since listing on the STAR Market. Measured from its intraday low of 404.03 yuan on Oct. 15, the share price has rebounded about 75% in less than six weeks.
Several other stocks in the sector strengthened in tandem. Unitree Robotics-W and Huayang Intelligent recorded 20% limit-ups, while Estun, Yijiahe, Beite Technology and Tianqi Shares sealed their boards, and Leaderdrive, Shuanglin and Best gained more than 10%. Fund-flow data showed that about half of humanoid robot concept stocks saw main-fund position increases on the day, with 12 stocks drawing net inflows of more than 100 million yuan (approximately $15.0 million) each. Victory Giant Technology topped the list with net inflows of 741 million yuan (approximately $111.2 million); the company, a leader in China's printed circuit board industry, has already developed PCBs dedicated to humanoid robots. CATL, Sanhua Intelligent Controls, Estun, Everwin Precision and Unitree Robotics-W also saw net inflows above 100 million yuan.
Developments on the industry side provided another layer of support. Tesla CEO Elon Musk, in a recent video-linked interview, gave a more specific timetable for Optimus, projecting that within the next 12 to 18 months the humanoid robot will be able to complete multi-step household chores such as taking out the trash, washing dishes and putting dishes away in cabinets, with a rollout path of "first heavy industry, then the home." The remarks pulled expectations for consumer-side humanoid robot applications from the distant future into the perceptible near term. Meanwhile, public demonstrations — a humanoid robot boxing match in Xiong'an and a global humanoid robot free-fighting league in Nanjing — also validated, from an engineering standpoint, the maturity of Chinese-made robots in dynamic balance and motion control.
Shipment forecasts were revised upward in tandem. In its August special report on physical AI, Goldman Sachs raised its forecast for global humanoid robot shipments in 2026 from 25,000 to 75,000 units, and projected about 890,000 units in 2030 and about 6.5 million in 2035, corresponding to a market of about $138.3 billion. Morgan Stanley's September report raised its 2026 China shipment forecast from 28,000 to 50,000 units and projected 446,000 units by 2030. Data from China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology show that China's humanoid robot output was about 20,000 units last year, exceeded 40,000 units in the first half of this year, and is expected to top 100,000 units for the full year.
Wanlian Securities believes the humanoid robot industry is at the dawn of a transition from technological breakthroughs to large-scale commercialization. On the supply side, Tesla, Unitree Robotics, AgiBot and UBTech are steadily advancing their mass-production pace; with policy and capital working together and AI large models continuously injecting capabilities into robots, the industry is expected to gradually move from the enterprise market toward consumers.
Order momentum and research interest in supply-chain companies are also rising. Since November, nearly 20 concept stocks have drawn institutional research visits; Kinco received 173 institutions during the month and said it has already achieved volume shipments in emerging markets such as humanoid and collaborative robots, with its client-side share steadily expanding, while in industrial robots it continues to develop global leading manufacturers and high-end Chinese customers. On the ratings front, excluding companies that posted losses in the first three quarters of this year, 13 concept stocks have ratings from at least 10 institutions, and analysts unanimously expect their net profit growth to exceed 20% in both 2026 and 2027. Among them, CATL has ratings from 41 institutions, the most of any, with institutions projecting net profit growth of 24.75% and 20.45% for 2026 and 2027, respectively.
Unitree Robotics' fundamentals partly support the market narrative. Its third-quarter report shows revenue of 1.817 billion yuan (approximately $272.7 million) in the first three quarters, up 55.71% year on year and already exceeding the full-year 2025 level; third-quarter revenue alone was 665 million yuan (approximately $99.8 million), with growth accelerating to 69.93%. Over the same period, net profit excluding non-recurring items fell 18.78% year on year, and gross margin slipped to 54.02% from 60.44% a year earlier, mainly reflecting a deliberate step-up in R&D spending — third-quarter R&D expenses jumped 249.58% year on year, directed at embodied AI large models and computing power.
Divergence among funds was already visible on the limit-up board, however. Exchange filings show Unitree Robotics had total buys of 689 million yuan (approximately $103.4 million) and total sells of 633 million yuan (approximately $95.0 million) on the day, for net buying of just 55.5497 million yuan (approximately $8.3 million). China International Capital Corporation's Shanghai branch led with net buying of 205 million yuan (approximately $30.8 million), CITIC Securities' Shanghai branch bought a net 159 million yuan (approximately $23.9 million), and institutional seats bought 125 million yuan (approximately $18.8 million); Goldman Sachs (China) Securities' Shanghai Pudong New Area Century Avenue seat sold 213 million yuan (approximately $32.0 million) the same day, and UBS Securities' Shanghai Huayuan Shiqiao Road seat sold 76.2 million yuan (approximately $11.4 million).
Market participants are anchoring the short-term watch window on whether Unitree Robotics' fourth-quarter orders materialize and whether gross margin can hold above 50%, with the medium-term watershed being whether the "one to two year" embodied intelligence inflection point cited by founder Wang Xingxing can be delivered. Angel investor and AI expert Guo Tao said the industry's opportunities stem from manufacturers' cost-reduction needs, iteration of embodied large models and the maturing of the Chinese supply chain, with industrial, special inspection and research/education applications likely to form viable markets first; challenges center on pressure to cut whole-machine costs, technical bottlenecks in dexterous manipulation and generalization across general-purpose tasks, the long payback period for industrial-scenario investment, and intensifying competition as automakers and AI giants pile in.

deep-tech-1fe7bf180d.headline: China’s Z.ai ‘aggressively’ using looped transformer method to improve AI models
deep-tech-1fe7bf180d.fulltext:

After Nvidia, will AMD be a target as China’s ‘2nd-choice’ supplier for AI chips?
Chinese artificial intelligence company Z.ai has credited an emerging technique – one that has drawn scrutiny from AI safety researchers – with helping its newly released flagship model achieve significant performance gains over its predecessor while improving computational efficiency.
The release marks the first time a Chinese AI company has disclosed using a “looped transformer” architecture in a major model, following recent reports that US giant OpenAI adopted the same method for its newest models.
In a blog post, Z.ai, also known as Zhipu AI, said it “aggressively” applied the technique over the past three months, enabling its GLM-5.4 model to match the performance of AI models two to four times its size.
“This lets us raise the intelligence ceiling with a relatively small compute overhead,” the company said, noting that the technique drove improvements in mathematics, science and coding, though it withheld the detailed benchmark scores typically published alongside major model releases.
While standard transformers, the dominant architecture behind AI breakthroughs in recent years, process new data through each layer of its internal neural network once, a looped transformer passes data through the same layers multiple times.
This creates a deeper reasoning network without substantially increasing parameter count or computing costs.
That efficiency offers an edge as the global AI industry races towards massive, trillion-parameter models, which tend to deliver stronger capabilities but are vastly more expensive to train and run.
Unlike domestic rivals such as Moonshot AI and DeepSeek, Z.ai has yet to release a flagship trillion-parameter model. GLM-5.4 retains the same 750-billion-parameter size as its predecessor, GLM-5.3, but performs at a level equivalent to a model in the 2 trillion to 3 trillion parameter range, according to Z.ai.
A significant scale-up also appears to be imminent. Z.ai hinted on Monday that its next model would be “significantly larger” and ready “soon”.
That aligns with a JPMorgan research note published last week, which cited an internal road map shared by Z.ai management indicating GLM-5.4 would be used to “verify training performance” ahead of a 3-trillion-parameter release by year-end aimed at “reaching the global frontier”.
Despite its efficiency gains, the looped transformer method has sparked debate over AI safety oversight and the risks of “black box” systems escaping human control.
Conventional reasoning models “think” out loud in human-readable text before generating a final answer or action, allowing researchers to monitor their logic for unwanted behaviour such as deception.
Because looped transformers reuse parts of internal neural layers, safety experts warn that a model’s decision-making process can become hidden inside those loops, making it largely opaque to human researchers.
Z.ai said GLM-5.4 spent fewer tokens on visible “thinking”, with average output length dropping up to 14 per cent on key benchmarks. “In effect, part of the reasoning shifts from explicit output tokens into the implicit depth of the loop,” the blog post said.
The safety debate gained momentum in September after US tech outlet The Information reported that OpenAI’s flagship GPT-6 Astra model would, for the first time, rely on a looped transformer to boost performance without inflating costs.
OpenAI did not confirm the report, though chief scientist Jakub Pachocki acknowledged safety concerns in subsequent social media posts, with a company representative calling the decline in model transparency “a real challenge that [it] takes seriously”.
Z.ai signalled similar caution on Monday. The company has restricted access to GLM-5.4 to its official chatbot website and coding service, saying it planned to open-source the model at an unspecified date “after completing necessary safety hardening”.
Vincent Chow is a technology reporter covering frontier AI models, AI governance and US-China competition. He previously covered Chinese society and was awarded a SOPA award for his culture reporting.

climate-energy-b44ab61dfd.headline: India set to miss 2030 EV adoption targets barring three-wheelers: BNEF
climate-energy-b44ab61dfd.fulltext:
India set to miss 2030 EV adoption targets barring three-wheelers: BNEF
India's EV market is growing rapidly, with passenger electric vehicle sales projected to rise 42% in 2026, but BloombergNEF says stronger policies and investment are needed to meet 2030 goals
Listen to This Article
India’s electric vehicle (EV) market is growing rapidly, but the country is set to miss its 2030 electrification targets across all vehicle segments except three-wheelers, according to a report by BloombergNEF (BNEF).
The report said while rising model availability, improving economics and supportive policies are driving adoption, stronger policy measures and investments will be needed to accelerate the transition.
BNEF's Economic Transition Scenario models a transition driven by market forces rather than additional policy interventions.
The assessment comes amid strong growth in EV sales. India's annual EV sales rose 17 per cent to surpass 2.4 million units in 2025 and already reached 2.9 million units in the first 10 months of 2026.
Electric two-wheeler sales got a boost from higher fossil fuel prices following the outbreak of the Iran war, the report said.
Also Read
Passenger EV sales are on track to exceed 305,000 units in 2026, a growth of 42 per cent over the previous year, with EVs accounting for 6.7 per cent of passenger vehicle sales in the segment.
BNEF expects passenger EV sales to nearly double to 621,000 units by 2030, accounting for 10.2 per cent of passenger vehicle sales.
Unlike several other automobile markets, private buyers are leading passenger EV adoption in India rather than shared mobility operators.
BNEF attributed this to the limited availability of affordable electric cars suitable for fleet operations and competition from compressed natural gas (CNG) vehicles, which also offer lower operating costs than petrol cars.
Electric two-wheelers accounted for 9.4 per cent of two-wheeler sales during January-October 2026. Annual sales are projected to exceed 4.5 million units by 2030.
However, scooters are expected to continue driving adoption, while relatively slow electrification of motorcycles will constrain growth in the overall segment.
Commercial vehicles present an even greater challenge. Just 1.5 per cent of medium and heavy commercial vehicle sales are projected to be electric by 2030, although the share could rise to 40.4 per cent by 2040.
Light commercial vehicles are expected to electrify faster, with EVs likely to account for 64 per cent of sales by 2040.
BNEF expects falling battery prices to make electric vehicles more affordable and accelerate mass-market adoption after 2030. Annual passenger EV sales could reach nearly 5.2 million units by 2040, while electric two-wheeler sales are projected at 13.2 million units.
The growing adoption of EVs is also expected to reshape India's fuel consumption.
BNEF projects that road fuel demand will peak at more than 2.5 million barrels per day in 2034 before declining to just over 2.3 million barrels per day by 2040.
Rising oil consumption by commercial vehicles is expected to be more than offset by reduced demand from passenger cars and two- and three-wheelers.
The transition will also require substantial charging infrastructure investments. India could need more than 8.7 million charging connectors by 2040, requiring an estimated $29 billion in investment.
Electricity demand for EV charging is projected to exceed 96 terawatt-hours by 2040, accounting for 6.8 per cent of the country's total electricity demand.
BNEF said lower operating costs, affordable models and improved charging access would support adoption in the near term.
However, stronger policy efforts and investment would be necessary to align India's road transport sector with a net-zero pathway by mid-century.

The developments highlight the importance of expanding energy storage capacity and wind power to improve the reliability of India’s electricity system.
Several European countries also achieved significant renewable energy milestones. In Sweden, wind and solar generation reached record shares, with wind power overtaking hydropower to become the country’s largest electricity source for the first time. Lower-than-normal reservoir levels following an exceptionally dry year contributed to the development. Increased wind generation also helped preserve hydropower reserves for periods of higher electricity demand.
Finland recorded a new wind power generation share of 42.2% in October. The country’s wind capacity more than tripled between 2020 and 2024. Together with nuclear power, growing wind generation has supported Finland’s transition away from coal-based electricity production. New Zealand also recorded higher contributions from wind and solar generation.
In the United Kingdom, wind and solar supplied a record 41% of electricity generation during the first nine months of 2026, compared with 25% from gas. Increased clean electricity generation has also helped reduce dependence on imported natural gas. The country reportedly saved an estimated £5.9 billion in gas imports following the beginning of the Hormuz crisis.
China recorded another decline in fossil fuel-based electricity generation in October. Thermal power generation fell 7.3%, marking the fourth consecutive monthly decline. Solar and wind generation increased by approximately one-third, while nuclear generation rose by one-fifth. However, China added 58.7 GW of new thermal power capacity during the first eight months of 2026, largely from coal-based projects, raising concerns about overcapacity.
Germany experienced a decline in its clean electricity share despite solar generation increasing by approximately 40% compared with October last year. Lower wind and hydropower generation, combined with a period of cold and cloudy weather, increased electricity production from coal and gas plants. This highlighted the need for additional renewable capacity, battery storage, flexible demand and stronger electricity interconnections.
Across OECD countries, clean electricity generation growth met the entire increase in electricity demand during the first nine months of 2026. However, fossil fuel generation declined only marginally, indicating the continued importance of accelerating renewable energy deployment.
The October records demonstrate the growing role of solar and wind power in global electricity systems. Solar generation has reportedly established a new global record somewhere in the world every month since January 2025. However, the latest developments also underline the need for energy storage, grid infrastructure and diversified renewable energy sources to ensure reliable electricity supplies.

India
Low fertilizer offtake, monsoon deficit likely to reduce wheat output
Currently, there has been a 15% decrease in the area sown with wheat across the country, prompting farmers to turn to other crops for better returns.
NEW DELHI: India’s wheat production outlook is expected to decline due to reduced soil moisture caused by weak Southwest and Northeast monsoons, which has also led to lower offtake of fertiliser. Currently, there has been a 15% decrease in the area sown with wheat across the country, prompting farmers to turn to other crops for better returns.
“Certainly, compared to a normal year, there will be some reduction in production, but it will not be as significant as some are predicting,” said Suresh Kumar Chaudhari, Director General of the Fertilizers Association of India (FAI), in Delhi.
Reports indicate that wheat acreage will decline by over 6%, marking the highest decrease in over two decades. The current wheat acreage stands at around 50 lakh hectares, which is more than 15% less than the previous year. The most significant drop in acreage has occurred in Haryana, followed by Uttar Pradesh. In contrast, Madhya Pradesh has seen an increase in acreage compared to last year.
As the world’s second-largest producer of wheat, India plays a crucial role in the global market. A decrease in production could impact domestic food inflation as well as the international market. Additionally, paddy crops in Southern India face challenges due to large deficits in rainfall during both summer and winter seasons.
The potential decline in production is also indicated by a reduced off-take of fertilizers, despite higher stocks of various fertilizers compared to the previous year. Between April and October 2026, consumption of major fertilizers decreased: Urea by around 4%, Nitrogen-Phosphorus-Potassium (NPK) by over 25%, super phosphate by over 5%, and Muriate of Potash by 11%. However, di-Ammonium Phosphate (DAP) consumption increased by 1.6%. Experts explain that the limited supply of cheaper Urea has forced farmers to buy DAP at a higher price as a substitute.
“The trend will be almost similar,” said S Sankarasubramanian, Chairman of FAI and MD & CEO of Coromandel International.

Pune: olee.space has been awarded a contract by the Defence Research & Development Organisation (DRDO), Ministry of Defence, to develop a laser-link drone communication system. The system will carry secure, high-speed data both ways between ground stations and drones in flight.
In the Russia–Ukraine war, radio jamming became so effective that drones began flying with kilometres of fibre-optic cable trailing behind them just to stay connected. The cables can’t be jammed, but they limit range and can snag or break.
Laser links offer the same advantage without the tether. Data travels on a narrow beam of light through open air. The result is fibre-like speed, impossible to interception, and no vulnerability to radio jamming.
Under the contract, olee.space will indigenously design and develop complete ground and airborne FSOC terminals with automatic Pointing, Acquisition and Tracking (PAT) within 18 months. The system pairs a tripod-mounted ground terminal with a compact optical payload integrated into a drone, providing a high-bandwidth, full-duplex link over long line-of-sight ranges.
James Solomon, Co-founder, olee.space, said, “Holding a laser link on a moving drone is one of the hardest problems in communications, and olee.space is one of very few companies globally working on this capability. We launched this programme a year ago, and we’re proud to have DRDO’s trust. This is Aatmanirbhar Bharat in action: frontier technology, built in India, competing with the world.”
olee.space is a Pune-based deep-tech company building laser communication systems for defence, aerospace and critical infrastructure. It does all of its work in-house, from optical design to field trials, to make secure, jam-proof laser links practical on the ground, in the air and in space.

EU plans sports ban in sweeping new Russia sanctions proposal
Proposed sanctions aim to curb Russian crypto financing and ‘propaganda’ in sports.
The European Commission has proposed new sanctions against Russia targeting its banks, crypto platforms, and participation in sporting events.
Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen introduced the 22nd package of sanctions on Monday, which includes a ban on Russian teams and individual athletes competing under the country’s flag at events in the European Union.
“We are striking harder at Russia’s ways to finance its war, by targeting its banks and crypto platforms,” von der Leyen wrote in a post on X, adding that the EU will be “shutting the door to its participation in European sports and cultural events”.
Economic pressure
Von der Leyen said 60 banks will be removed from the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) messaging system used for international payments under the new proposals, which are intended to maintain economic pressure on Russia, almost five years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
She announced the creation of a crypto sanctions task force seeking to curb countries helping Russia to evade sanctions.
The commission also proposed a ban on visas for Russians who had fought in the war in Ukraine.
“Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries,” von der Leyen said.
‘Propaganda activities’
The plan also put forward restrictions on financial flows from Russian sponsors to sports and cultural associations based in the EU. Russian nationals would also no longer be allowed to hold leadership positions on the governing bodies of sports federations.
“Sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities,” said von der Leyen.
The proposed package must be endorsed by all 27 EU member countries before going into force and comes just over a month after the bloc posted the largest listing of sanctions against Russia, targeting about 1,600 Russian officials and companies linked to its arms industry.
The EU has already slapped sanctions on more than 4,200 people and entities, including Russian President Vladimir Putin and several energy companies.

science-mind-af1584915d.headline: A shared meaning component across languages in the human brain
science-mind-af1584915d.fulltext:
Abstract
Human languages differ profoundly in their sounds, words and grammatical systems, yet all support the communication of complex meanings. How the brain handles this diversity remains a fundamental question in language neuroscience. Multilingual neural network models offer a way to answer this question by representing linguistic content across languages in a shared space. Leveraging these advances, we evaluated the similarity of linguistic representations in speakers of 21 languages. Here we combined existing (12 languages across 4 language families) and newly collected functional magnetic resonance imaging data (9 languages across 4 families) to test encoding models predicting brain activity in the language network using representations from multilingual models. Model representations predicted brain responses reliably within each language. Critically, encoding models trained on one set of languages generalized zero-shot to previously unseen languages, accurately predicting neural responses without exposure to the target language. This cross-lingual generalization extended across variation in language family, stimulus type and presentation modality. These findings point to a shared cross-lingual component for meaning across human languages.
