science-mind-d549df7ebf.headline: Brain Speech Hub Builds a "Blueprint" Before We Speak
science-mind-d549df7ebf.fulltext:
Summary:
Neuroscientists have overturned a century-old textbook model of human language, revealing that a key speech comprehension region inside Wernicke’s area also generates an abstract “blueprint” for upcoming words a quarter-second before we speak. The study shows that listening and speaking neurons sit side by side, opening new targets for neurosurgical mapping, autism research, and brain-computer interfaces that restore speech.
Key Facts:
- Rewriting the Language Textbook: Contrary to the classic model separating speech comprehension from speech production, researchers found that neurons in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG), a core part of Wernicke’s area, activate roughly 250 milliseconds before speaking to assemble a structural plan for intended words.
- Word Blueprints Before Vocal Movement: Rather than encoding individual sounds or mouth movements, lpSTG neurons encode abstract word features, including word length, syllable count, and word frequency, before passing the blueprint forward to frontal speech-planning areas and the motor cortex.
- New Target for Speech Brain-Computer Interfaces: Because speech-listening and speech-planning neurons coexist side by side in the lpSTG, researchers successfully decoded both attempted and heard words in two paralyzed participants, offering a promising alternative BCI target when motor speech areas are damaged.
Source: UC San Francisco
For more than a century, neuroscience textbooks have divided human language into two separate anatomical compartments: Wernicke’s area in the temporal lobe to understand heard speech, and frontal motor circuits (such as Broca’s area and the motor cortex) to produce spoken words.
Yet that neat division never fully explained a persistent clinical paradox: why patients who suffer strokes or injuries in Wernicke’s area frequently struggle not only to comprehend language, but also to retrieve and speak the words they intend to say.
Now, in a landmark study published in Science, researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) led by neurosurgeon Dr. Edward Chang have resolved that 150-year-old puzzle.
Drawing on 15 years of high-resolution intracranial brain recordings alongside targeted neural experiments, the team demonstrated that a specialized hub within Wernicke’s area actively generates a cognitive “blueprint” for each word roughly a quarter-second before a person begins to speak.
Updating a 150-Year-Old Neurological Hypothesis
In the 1870s, German neurologist Carl Wernicke originally speculated that the posterior temporal lobe housed an “auditory image of words”, an internal template that could guide spoken output. Over subsequent decades, however, because the region sits nestled inside auditory cortex, neuroscientists largely pigeonholed it as purely a passive receiver for incoming speech sounds.
“What’s different now is that we finally have the tools and the data to see the brain at the speed and scale at which speech actually happens — millisecond by millisecond, down to individual neurons,” explained co-first author Dr. Matthew Leonard, associate professor of neurological surgery at UCSF.
Combining longitudinal intracranial recordings gathered in Chang’s laboratory with new experiments designed to separate listening from speaking, Leonard and co-first author Dr. Alex Silva, a student in UCSF’s Medical Scientist Training Program, pinpointed a crucial cortical hub: the left posterior superior temporal gyrus (lpSTG).
Inside the Quarter-Second Word Blueprint
Tracking neural activity at millisecond resolution revealed that specific populations of neurons inside the lpSTG surged into action approximately 250 milliseconds (a quarter-second) before vocalization began.
Crucially, this pre-speech firing did not represent raw acoustic sounds or physical movements of the lips and tongue. Instead, lpSTG neurons constructed an abstract linguistic blueprint encoding:
- Word length
- Number of syllables
- Lexical frequency (how common the word is in English)
Once assembled in the lpSTG, this structural blueprint traveled forward to speech-planning networks in the frontal lobe, and subsequently to the motor cortex, which translated the plan into precise articulatory muscle commands. Furthermore, high-resolution mapping showed that neurons dedicated to hearing speech sit directly beside, and sometimes overlap with, the neurons generating outgoing word blueprints.
“This changes the textbook view of how the brain perceives and produces speech,” said Chang, chair of the UCSF Department of Neurological Surgery and member of the UCSF Weill Institute for Neurosciences. “Instead of being separate systems, the processes of hearing speech and actually speaking are very intertwined.”
Implications for Child Language, Autism, and Speech BCIs
Housing incoming auditory processing and outgoing word planning inside the same microcircuit provides a compelling neural mechanism for how infants acquire language, converting heard sounds directly into motor-ready speech blueprints. It also offers a targeted anatomical region to investigate why roughly one-quarter to one-third of autistic children remain minimally verbal despite demonstrating strong language comprehension.
“It gives us a specific place in the brain to look, and a specific question to ask,” Chang noted.
Equally transformative are the implications for neurotechnology. Today’s speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) typically decode intended words from the motor cortex, a strategy that fails if a patient’s motor pathways are severely damaged. Because the lpSTG operates upstream of motor execution, it offers an alternative decoding gateway.
In proof-of-concept testing with two participants living with severe paralysis and anarthria (inability to speak), the UCSF team successfully decoded both the words participants attempted to say and the words they heard directly from lpSTG signals, pointing toward future conversational BCIs capable of capturing both sides of human dialogue.
Questions and Answers
How does this discovery change what we know about how the brain produces speech?
For over 100 years, textbooks taught that speech comprehension (Wernicke’s area) and speech production were handled by separate brain systems. UCSF researchers proved that a region inside Wernicke’s area (the lpSTG) actually activates a quarter-second before we speak to build an abstract “blueprint” of each intended word, including its length and syllable count, before sending it to motor areas.
Why can damage to Wernicke’s area make it hard to speak words, not just understand them?
Because the neurons that process heard speech sit directly alongside the neurons that build the structural blueprint for spoken words in the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, a stroke or injury to that region disrupts both language comprehension and word planning.
How could this finding help paralyzed patients communicate?
Current speech brain-computer interfaces read signals from the brain’s motor cortex, which can be damaged in some paralyzed patients. Because the lpSTG creates word blueprints earlier in the speech pipeline, decoding signals from this region could restore communication for a wider range of paralyzed individuals—and potentially capture both heard and spoken words for natural conversation.

science-mind-23b75ea76e.headline: Why We Slow Down With Age: Brain Serotonin Blocks Movement
science-mind-23b75ea76e.fulltext:
Summary:
Researchers have uncovered the specific brain circuit responsible for age-related declines in physical activity. The study reveals that aging increases serotonin signaling in motivation and movement centers, acting like a biological brake that suppresses dopamine-driven urges to move, while blocking this serotonin pathway restores youthful activity, speed, lean muscle mass, and grip strength in older mice.
Key Facts:
- A Brain Circuit Behind Slowing Down: Comparing adults aged 50–70 with younger adults aged 17–30, and mirroring the profile in mice, researchers found that age-related increases in brain serotonin signaling suppress dopamine pathways that motivate spontaneous physical movement.
- Releasing the “Serotonin Brake”: Rather than running out of physical fuel, the aging brain actively applies a stronger neurochemical brake on movement; blocking this specific serotonin pathway restored youthful activity levels and walking speed in aged mice.
- Systemic Body Composition Benefits: Releasing the brain’s serotonin brake in older mice not only boosted voluntary physical activity, but also reduced body fat accumulation, increased lean muscle mass, and improved grip strength.
Source: UKRI-BBSRC
Physical inactivity is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for chronic disease, frailty, and premature mortality. Yet across human populations and animal species alike, advancing age brings a predictable, progressive decline in spontaneous daily movement, a biological phenomenon whose root neural cause has remained largely unexplained.
In a new study published via ScienceDirect and supported by the UKRI-Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBSRC), researchers led by Professor Lora Heisler have identified a dedicated neurochemical circuit in the brain that actively dials down the natural drive to move as we grow older.
The Bicycle Analogy: Dopamine Pedals vs. Serotonin Brakes
To establish how movement patterns shift across the adult lifespan, the research team first compared physical behavior in adults aged 50 to 70 against younger adults aged 17 to 30. Older adults walked more slowly, covered less daily distance, and carried higher levels of body fat, a behavioral and metabolic trajectory closely mirrored by aging mice.
Probing the neural circuits governing motivation and motor initiation in the mouse brain, the investigators uncovered a fundamental shift in neurochemical balance:
- Dopamine Drives Movement: Dopaminergic pathways act as the brain’s motivational accelerator, generating the intrinsic urge to initiate physical movement.
- Serotonin Applies the Brake: With advancing age, signaling through a specific serotonin pathway intensifies within motivation and motor circuits, progressively suppressing dopamine activity and dampening voluntary physical drive.
“Think of the brain’s movement system as a bicycle. The brain chemical dopamine helps push the pedals, driving the urge to move, while another chemical called serotonin puts a brake on this pathway. With age, that brake becomes increasingly engaged, slowing voluntary movement. We found that releasing the brake restored more youthful levels of activity in older mice,” explained Professor Heisler.
“Rather than the aging brain running out of fuel, our findings suggest it may be applying too much brake. By reducing signalling through this serotonin pathway, we were able to release that brake and restore more youthful patterns of movement in older mice.”
Restoring Youthful Vitality and Muscle Strength
When the researchers experimentally blocked this age-amplified serotonin pathway in older mice, the physiological transformation extended well beyond increased step counts.
Releasing the neurochemical brake restored youthful spontaneous activity and movement speed, leading to measurable improvements in systemic physical health: treated older animals accumulated less body fat, gained lean muscle mass, and demonstrated stronger physical grip strength.
New Pathways for Healthy Aging
By demonstrating that age-related physical slowing is actively programmed by a modifiable brain circuit rather than inevitable muscular exhaustion, the research opens promising therapeutic avenues for extending healthspan and physical independence.
“Going forward, our findings suggest that targeting serotonin signalling in this pathway could one day provide new approaches to maintain mobility, independence, and healthy aging in an increasingly older population,” Heisler said.
“We all tend to slow down as we get older, but until now it hasn’t been clear why,” added Dr. Amanda Collis, Executive Director for Strategic Research and International at UKRI-BBSRC. “This BBSRC-supported research shows that part of the answer lies in the brain, identifying a pathway that appears to dial down our natural drive to be physically active with age.”
Questions and Answers
Why do people naturally become less physically active as they get older?
Researchers discovered that aging increases signaling in a specific serotonin pathway in the brain’s movement and motivation centers. This heightened serotonin acts like a brake that suppresses dopamine, the brain chemical that drives the natural urge to move, causing voluntary physical activity to slow down.
Can blocking this brain pathway reverse age-related slowing?
In studies with older mice, blocking this overactive serotonin pathway released the biological brake on dopamine. As a result, older animals regained youthful levels of physical activity and movement speed, accumulated less body fat, gained lean muscle mass, and improved their grip strength.
What does this discovery mean for healthy aging in humans?
Because the decline in daily movement is driven by an active brain circuit rather than the body simply “running out of fuel,” targeting this specific serotonin pathway could eventually lead to new therapies that help older adults stay active, independent, and healthy longer.

Brain serotonin circuit reverses decline in physical activity with age
Physical inactivity increases with age and is the fourth leading risk factor for mortality. Establishing the mechanisms underpinning declining activity with age has remained both elusive and difficult to overcome. Older (50–70 years old) compared with younger (17–30 years old) United Kingdom participants showed reduced physical activity, and this profile was effectively modelled in mice.
Analysis of brain serotonin neurons in the dorsal raphe (5-HTDR) revealed altered firing activity in older mice. Chemogenetically mimicking this 5-HTDR tone in young adult mice produced an older adult physical activity profile.

These data fill a longstanding knowledge gap by defining brain circuitry programming the decline in physical activity with age, and importantly, a means to reverse it.

work-careers-1e5f07c8a5.fulltext:
Layoffs and AI fears: 72% of India's tech workers want to switch careers
56% wouldn't steer their kids into tech, and just 4% would recommend software engineering to a young person starting out
Listen to This Article
India's technology sector, long regarded as one of the country's most attractive career destinations for its high salaries and global opportunities, is facing a growing crisis of confidence among its own workforce. As layoffs, restructuring and concerns about artificial intelligence reshape the industry, nearly three out of four technology professionals in India say they would switch to an entirely different career if given the opportunity.
A survey of 2,958 India-based professionals by anonymous workplace community platform Blind found that 72% would leave their current careers for a completely different profession if there were no financial costs or retraining requirements. 72% said they would switch to a completely different career tomorrow if it required no cost or retraining. The largest group, 42%, would make the move as long as the pay stayed the same. Only 13% said they are happy where they are.
While 30% said they would make the switch immediately, another 42% said they would do so if they could retain their existing salaries. Only 13% said they were happy with their current careers and would not consider leaving.
Also Read
The findings point to a growing disconnect between the financial rewards associated with technology jobs and professionals' long-term satisfaction and confidence in the sector.
The reluctance to remain in technology is also extending to the next generation. Around 56% of respondents said they would probably or definitely not encourage their children to pursue careers in tech. Nearly one in three, or 31%, said they would definitely discourage them.
" The urge to leave was strongest at Intuit (89%), Goldman Sachs (87%), PayPal (87%), Visa (86%), Expedia Group (83%). It ran nearly as high at Oracle (79%), which has reportedly cut about 12,000 jobs in India this year, as well as at Salesforce (79%) and Adobe (78%), where Blind users have reported silent layoffs in India. Even at Meta and Apple, where it was lowest, more than half would switch," the company said in a statement. 
The career shift has already shown up on Blind. With more than a month left in the year, posts written in India about leaving software engineering are up 37.5% from all of 2025. For a growing number of India's tech workers, the question is no longer which company to join next, but whether to stay in tech at all.
"They don’t want the next generation pursuing tech, either. 56% said they would definitely or probably not encourage their child to go into tech. Nearly 1 in 3 said definitely not. That view holds even at the companies young Indians most want to join. At Microsoft, the largest group of respondents, 67% would steer their child away from tech, and over 50% felt the same at Google and Amazon," said Blind in a release.
The survey comes amid continued restructuring across the technology industry, with concerns over job security, changing skill requirements and the impact of artificial intelligence influencing career decisions. Blind surveyed 2,958 India-based professionals between November 6 and 19, 2026. Company figures include only companies with at least 10 responses to the question.
Healthcare beats software engineering as preferred career choice
When asked which profession they would recommend to a young person starting out today, respondents showed a clear preference for careers they believe offer greater long-term stability or are less vulnerable to automation.
Medical and healthcare careers emerged as the most preferred option, selected by 34% of respondents.
Artificial intelligence and machine learning came second, with 19%, followed by government and public sector jobs at 15%.
Other technology roles, including data, cybersecurity and hardware, accounted for 10% of responses. Law and finance also received 10%, while arts and teaching were chosen by 8%.
Software engineering ranked last, with just 4% of respondents recommending it as a career choice.
Notably, not a single respondent from Google, Meta or NVIDIA selected software engineering as their preferred career recommendation for young people.
The preference for healthcare and public sector careers suggests that professionals are increasingly weighing factors beyond salary, including job security, resilience to technological disruption and long-term earning potential.
AI creates a career paradox
The survey also highlights an interesting contradiction in how technology workers view artificial intelligence.
While software engineering received only 4% of recommendations, AI and machine learning emerged as the second-most preferred career path, attracting 19% of responses.
This suggests that professionals are not necessarily turning away from technology altogether. Instead, they may be reassessing which technology skills and roles will remain valuable as AI adoption accelerates.
The preference for healthcare, government employment and specialised technology functions also reflects a growing interest in careers perceived to offer more durable opportunities.
Asked which path they would most recommend to someone starting out today, respondents leaned toward work AI cannot easily replace, or into AI itself. Medicine and healthcare led at 34%, and 15% picked government or public sector jobs. AI and machine learning came second at 19%. In a Blind thread on which profession has the highest earning potential over a lifetime in India, an Apple employee replied: "IAS (civil services) followed by IPS. Earn more than politicians, never get voted out." In another thread, a Cisco employee listed hands-on jobs: "Landscaper. Plumber. Hvac technician. Dentist. Veterinarian. Physical therapist. Nurse."
The findings come at a time when businesses are increasingly integrating AI into software development and other functions, raising questions about the future demand for traditional technology roles.
However, the survey does not establish that AI has directly caused professionals to consider leaving the industry. Job insecurity, workplace satisfaction, compensation and changing career expectations could also influence these responses.
The Blind survey was conducted between November 6 and November 19, 2026, among 2,958 India-based professionals. Company-level figures include only employers with at least 10 responses to the relevant question.
Separately, Blind used its AI tool Clair to analyse discussions posted between January 1, 2025, and November 17, 2026, about leaving technology or software engineering for a different career.

South Korea scrambled fighter jets and briefly issued an air-raid warning for an island after multiple Russian warplanes entered its air defence identification zone, the latest in a series of such incidents.
The defence ministry said it would summon Russia’s military attaché on Tuesday morning to lodge a protest over the incident.
The Russian aircraft entered the air defence identification zone over the East Sea, also known as the Sea of Japan, and "departed as our forces were taking military measures”, including deploying fighter jets, the ministry said.
Seoul did not immediately say how many or what type of Russian aircraft it had detected.
A mix-up over emergency alerts caused confusion for an estimated 9,000 residents of Ulleung Island, 130km east of the Korean peninsula, after the interior ministry erroneously reported that warplanes had breached South Korea’s territorial airspace.
The air-raid warning, issued at 7.52am, urged residents to evacuate to underground shelters. It was lifted three minutes later, with authorities saying the aircraft had left the area.
The North Gyeongsang provincial government compounded the confusion by sending out a separate message stating the warning had been lifted but mistakenly identifying the Russian jets as suspected North Korean aircraft. The government issued a correction only about 40 minutes later.
"It was Russian aircraft that violated the airspace. We inform that it was Russian aircraft," it said, without explaining the reason for the error.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff subsequently clarified that the Russian aircraft had entered the air defence identification zone but had not violated the country’s territorial airspace.
“Some media reports that ‘a flying object believed to be a North Korean aircraft violated South Korean airspace’ are not true,” it said in a brief statement.
The air defence identification zone extends beyond a country’s territorial airspace and is used to find and monitor approaching aircraft for national security purposes.
A breach of South Korea’s territorial airspace by foreign military jets would mark a major escalation in tensions with Seoul.
The erroneous identification of the aircraft as North Korean could have heightened tensions between the two Koreas, which remain technically at war.
South Korea’s military spokesperson, Jang Do Young, said the Russian aircraft had flown close to the territorial airspace around Ulleung Island, prompting the military to coordinate with the government over the evacuation alert.
Mr Jang did not directly answer when asked whether a miscommunication with the safety ministry had led to the erroneous warning, saying the military needed to look into the matter further.
He said that the North Gyeongsang government may have mistakenly sent out a text message intended for a training exercise.
The incident is the latest in a string of similar encounters. On 17 November, South Korea scrambled fighter jets after Russian aircraft entered the air defence identification zone over the East Sea. The planes left without entering South Korean territorial airspace.
The same day, Japan reported that suspected Russian jets had briefly entered its airspace and lodged a protest with Moscow.

Nato chief Mark Rutte said Monday the alliance would defend against threats in space when asked about German media reports that Russia may be preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.
The media reports, citing unnamed German military and BND spy agency sources, said Moscow was thought to be planning such a launch in the coming weeks, giving it the capability to destroy other satellites.
The Russian embassy in Berlin characterised the claims as “groundless allegations,” Tass news agency reported, calling it “part of a propaganda campaign aimed at smearing Russia”.
Rutte, asked about the reports while visiting Berlin, vowed: “We will always make sure that we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure that we are safe when it comes to the space element”.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, speaking alongside Rutte, did not confirm or deny the media reports but voiced concern.
“Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking,” he said.
“They reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue,” added Merz, whose chancellery oversees the BND foreign intelligence agency.
A German government spokesman said that the reports were being taken “very seriously”, though he did not confirm them either and warned against causing “excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers”.
Public broadcasters WDR and NDR, along with the Sueddeutsche Zeitung daily, reported that Russia planned to launch a satellite dubbed “Sputnik-S” equipped with a nuclear warhead sometime in the coming weeks.
The outlets, citing unnamed sources, said that the intelligence reports about the plans had recently been shared among several Nato countries and that the German government had been briefed on the matter.
The satellite had been stored in the Moscow region, according to the news outlets, and could be used to disrupt or destroy important communications and observation satellites orbiting Earth.
Josef Aschbacher, head of the European Space Agency, described the presence of nuclear weapons in space as “the ultimate nightmare scenario” in comments to the Handelsblatt newspaper.
Rutte had already voiced concern about Russia’s nuclear plans in April 2025. “We are aware of reports that Russia is exploring the possibility of deploying nuclear weapons in space,” he told the Sunday edition of the German newspaper Die Welt at the time.
The BND declined to comment, while Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, questioned after a meeting with his Ukrainian counterpart, said that it was “too early to speculate publicly”, in particular because “the nature of these nuclear weapons is not clear”.
“We are consulting internally and taking the measures that need to be taken,” he said.
The Foreign Office in Berlin stated that the deployment of a nuclear weapon in space would constitute “a flagrant breach of the 1967 Outer Space Treaty”.
Together with allies and partners, Germany tabled a resolution in the United Nations General Assembly in 2004 calling for compliance with the Outer Space Treaty and for the renunciation of the development of such weapons.
The US military’s Defence Intelligence Agency warned in a report released in October that Russia is “developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon”.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he had not seen the latest news stories on the topic but that frequent reports citing “unknown sources” are “hardly worth taking seriously”.
Russia has always denied developing a nuclear weapon for space. Moscow is categorically opposed to the deployment of nuclear weapons in space, President Vladimir Putin said in February 2024.
Even at that time, US representatives were alleging that Russia was working on such a weapon. Various satellites came under scrutiny – among others Kosmos-2553, launched in 2022, which, according to Russian sources, was intended to investigate the effects of radiation and heavily charged particles.
In 2025, the German Foundation for Science and Policy (SVP) concluded that Kosmos-2553 was not an active anti-satellite weapon. While many observers considered it plausible that Russia was pursuing a nuclear-armed anti-satellite programme, there was no evidence to support this, it said.
The project most likely to resemble an anti-satellite weapon was the Zeus project, the scientist Dmitri Stefanovich of the Russian Academy of Sciences said in 2024. This is said to be a nuclear-powered space probe being developed as a towing vehicle for lunar missions.
The Russian news agency RIA Novosti also reported on this project, stating that it was intended to be capable of disabling other satellites using electromagnetic radiation.

world-9e8a6a2e3d.headline: Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
world-9e8a6a2e3d.fulltext:
Nato chief vows defence against space threat after Russian nuclear satellite reports
- Published
Nato chief Mark Rutte has said the alliance will defend against any threats in space after reports that Russia was preparing to launch a nuclear-armed satellite.
Intelligence reports about a possible launch in the next 60 days had been shared among Nato countries this month, according to German media outlets. It was not clear which country had authored the reports.
Asked about the reports, Rutte said: "We will always make sure we defend every inch of Nato territory, and that includes making sure we are safe when it comes to the space element."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said he hadn't seen the latest reports but dismissed reports citing "unknown sources" as "hardly worth taking seriously".
The Russian embassy in Berlin told German media it rejected what it called "unfounded allegations" and said the reports were part of a "propaganda campaign".
Rutte told the press conference in Berlin that Nato had a variety of response options.
"When it comes to the military domain, we will always make assessments of our deterrence and defence and make updates where necessary," he said.
Citing anonymous German military and intelligence sources, the reports by broadcasters NDR and WDR, and newspaper Sueddeutsche Zeitung, said the Russian satellite was dubbed "Sputnik-S" and was equipped with a nuclear warhead. It could be used to disrupt or destroy other satellites, including important communication and observation satellites.
Standing alongside Rutte, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz did not confirm or deny the reports of Russia's plans, but said they "reveal the level of escalation Russia is evidently prepared to pursue".
"Reports that Russia is planning to introduce nuclear weaponry into space are not new, yet they remain no less shocking," he said.
A German government spokesman earlier also did not confirm or deny the reports, but said it was taking the reports "very seriously", AFP reported. The spokesman, however, warned against causing "excessive nervousness regarding hypothetical dangers".
Josef Aschbacher, the head of the European Space Agency, said having nuclear weapons in space was "the ultimate nightmare scenario", German paper Handelsblatt reported.
Russia is a signatory to the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, which bans weapons of mass destruction from orbit. Other countries, including the US and China, have deployed or plan to deploy other weapons in space, exploring other capabilities outside of the treaty, such as targeting rivals' satellites - which are key for military communications, surveillance and navigation.
In 2024 the US claimed Russia was developing a "space-based" anti-satellite weapon armed with a nuclear warhead. Russia denied the accusation.
"Our position is clear and transparent. We have always been categorically against the deployment of nuclear weapons in space and we are still against it," President Vladimir Putin said at the time.
In September the US Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said the US had "on-orbit, space-control weapons" circling the planet, but did not provide specifics. In response to the announcement, the Kremlin's Peskov told Russian media that space "must be free of any weapon".

deep-tech-ba7c69d276.headline: Ukraine claims drone strikes on Russian ships off Libya: What do we know?
deep-tech-ba7c69d276.fulltext:
Ukraine claims drone strikes on Russian ships off Libya: What do we know?
Drone strikes on two Russian vessels near Libyan coast fuels fears of Ukraine war’s spread.
Ukraine has claimed responsibility for sinking a Russian warship and striking a cargo vessel off Libya’s coast, raising concerns about the Russia-Ukraine war widening geographically.
“It all took place off the coast of Libya. Our warriors deployed seven Ukrainian-made naval drones,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a post on X on Monday.
The attack targeted the Russian corvette Merkury and the cargo vessel MV Angara, which Zelenskyy said was used to transport weapons.
The attacks come amid an intensifying Ukrainian campaign targeting Russian naval assets, energy infrastructure and vessels linked to Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet, which helps Russia circumvent Western sanctions.
The developments have also raised questions about the involvement of foreign powers in a divided Libya, and the risk of drawing other nations into the conflict, nearly five years after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Here is what we know about the attacks, who may be behind them and what they mean for the expanding reach of the war.
What do we know about the attacks?
The Russian Navy’s Merkury was struck at the Benghazi naval base in eastern Libya on Sunday, triggering an explosion and fire.
Satellite imagery showed most of the corvette had capsized and sunk, with only its bow visible above water.
Zelenskyy confirmed the sinking on Monday, saying a Russian Kamov Ka-27 military helicopter was also destroyed.
“Our second target was the Russian dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA, which the enemy used to transport weapons. Result: target hit,” he added.
A day earlier, the Russian cargo ship Sparta II was struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland. The vessel caught fire and drifted into Finnish waters. All 16 crew members were evacuated, with one slightly injured.
In Finland, the military assessed the vessel was likely struck by Ukraine. Russian authorities said two drones hit the Sparta II in international waters. Kyiv has not publicly claimed responsibility for Sunday’s attack.
Zelenskyy said his country would continue to launch operations in designated maritime areas in response to Russia’s aggression.
Kyiv’s attacks come as Russia has intensified its air attacks across Ukraine, using ballistic missiles, drones and guided bombs. Energy facilities, bridges, Black Sea ports and other civilian infrastructure have been targeted in Ukraine, which has countered with attacks on Russian energy sites and other targets.
What have Libya and Russia said?
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov described Ukraine’s attacks off the coast of Libya, as well as the targeting of Russian cargo vessels in the Baltic Sea, as a “very dangerous trend”.
Peskov warned Ukraine of “painful” consequences. “The Defence Ministry is dealing with this matter, and information will also be provided through the Defence Ministry if deemed appropriate,” he said.
Libya’s eastern administration condemned the attack as a violation of its sovereignty and said it had requested an international investigation through the United Nations.
“The Libyan government will not allow Libyan ports, territory or territorial waters to be turned into an arena for settling scores or exporting international conflicts,” it said.
Saddam Haftar, son of renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar, said Libya’s security and sovereignty are a “national responsibility that cannot tolerate political posturing or the exploitation of incidents to promote accusations and stir up fears”.
“Rather, it requires prioritising the national interest and dealing responsibly with everything that affects our country’s security and stability,” he said in a statement on Facebook.
The rival UN-recognised government in Tripoli also commented on the incident, saying it was concerned by “risks posed by involving civilian ports and facilities in activities linked to external conflicts”.
Meanwhile, the UN has called for an independent investigation into Sunday’s drone attacks.
On Monday, the UN Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”.
“Libya cannot afford and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts,” UNSMIL wrote in a post on X.
The oil-rich nation has been divided between the government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east since the overthrow of longtime ruler Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.
In September, Libya denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base in the northwest of the country to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The origin of Sunday’s attack is still not confirmed.
How many Russian vessels have been attacked in recent weeks?
At least four Russian vessels have reportedly been targeted in November, including the Merkury, MV Angara and Sparta II.
The Finnish military also reported detecting a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland in the Baltic Sea during Ukrainian drone attacks the previous week.
In March, a Russian LNG tanker sank off Libya’s coast following an attack Moscow blamed on Ukraine.
In December 2025, Ukraine claimed responsibility for striking a Russian-linked oil tanker in the Mediterranean.
Is the Ukraine-Russia war expanding geographically?
Academic Alexey D Muraviev says the conflict has already expanded beyond Ukraine.
“The Mediterranean has firmly become an external theatre of operations, particularly maritime operations,” Muraviev, senior research fellow in defence and strategic studies at Edith Cowan University, told Al Jazeera.
He said the vessels targeted in Libyan and Finnish territories were likely involved in transporting military equipment or other supplies to Africa, potentially supporting Russia’s Africa Corps, which operates alongside Moscow-aligned governments.
Muraviev said Ukrainian forces had previously confronted Russian security personnel in Africa, demonstrating that the conflict had already extended beyond its original battlefield.
“Even in this sense, there have been cases when the war in Ukraine effectively extended onto the African continent,” he said.
The sinking of the Merkury, commissioned in 2023, would also weaken Russia’s naval capabilities, Muraviev said.
However, the academic warned that the Gulf of Finland was particularly sensitive because of its geography and the proximity of Russian and NATO forces.
“In my personal view, it is an area where a possible clash between Russia and NATO is quite possible,” he said.
Muraviev added that the attacks could have wider implications for global shipping, which is already facing heightened security threats around the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandeb.
“[The attacks] just add additional risks to marine operators from across the world,” he said.

world-36e9ed3631.headline: Ukraine confirms it used naval drones to strike two Russian ships off Libya
world-36e9ed3631.fulltext:
Ukraine has confirmed it deployed naval drones in strikes on two Russian vessels off Libya on Sunday, including one that sank the corvette Merkury, one of Russia’s newest vessels.
Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, said seven domestically made naval drones were launched from a mothership in the operation, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy described as “exemplary”.
“We continue our operations in designated waters. We are responding to Russia’s aggression. We are developing Ukrainian weapons,” the Ukrainian president added.
Zelenskyy released video footage, filmed by an approaching drone, showing the drones as they smashed into the side of the warship at its berth in the Benghazi naval base, triggering huge explosions that lit up the night sky.
In its own statement, the SBU said: “The defence forces of Ukraine have once again demonstrated that the Russian military fleet and its logistics networks have no safe routes, even far beyond the Black Sea.”
Zelenskyy said the other vessel hit on Sunday, the dry cargo ship MV Angara, was being used by Russia to transport weapons.
The operation, conducted 1,500 miles (2,400km) from the frontline in Ukraine, was the latest daring long-range assault by Kyiv’s forces. Last week Ukraine hit the Kerch bridge – a key supply line to Russian-occupied Crimea – and the Russian Baltic seaport of Kaliningrad.
Residents in Benghazi heard loud explosions and saw flames at the naval base early on Sunday. Civil defence units rushed to the site and extinguished the fire, authorities in eastern Libya said.
The Institute for the Study of War said the Merkury had stopped over for several days, under a cooperation agreement, to refuel and resupply as it escorted Russian cargo ships that could carry military supplies en route to Russia.
The Merkury had docked to refuel and take on supplies as part of a cooperation agreement between Russia and the eastern-based government in Libya, the statement said without providing details about the vessel or its cargo.
Vladimir Putin had taken a personal interest in the ship. In 2019 he toured the St Petersburg yard where it was being built and backed naming it after a tsarist-era brig celebrated for fighting off two Turkish warships in the Black Sea in 1829.
At the 2023 Navy Day parade, the Russian president singled it out among 30 new vessels as evidence that Russia was “consistently building up the power of its fleet”. He hailed its St George flag as “a sign of the inviolability of our naval traditions” and said it was “gratifying” that the brig’s name had been revived.
Russian state media also talked up the ship. The news agency Tass called it the “newest missile corvette”, while the channel TV Tsentr claimed its stealth technology made it “invisible to radar”.
Divided Libya has emerged in recent years as a proxy battlefield. Moscow has long supported the breakaway government in Benghazi of Khalifa Haftar in its efforts to use eastern Libya as a staging post for its military presence in north Africa and the Sahel.
More recently there have been reports of increasing Ukrainian operations. In April, Associated Press reported that Ukrainian drone specialists had been operating at military sites in Misrata, Tripoli and Zawiya in Libya’s west. In September Libyan authorities denied reports by CNN that it allowed Ukraine to use a military base to launch drones against vessels from Russia’s “shadow fleet” in the Mediterranean.
The confirmation that Ukraine was behind the attacks was condemned by the UN-recognised government in Tripoli. It said Libya rejected any foreign military operations on its territory or in its waters.
There was no immediate comment from Russia about the strikes. The UN mission in Libya (UNSMIL), however, expressed “serious concern” over the attacks, calling for “an immediate, independent and transparent investigation”. It said on X: “Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts.”
Ukraine prides itself on its military industry, particularly its progress in drone technology, which it has extensively developed since Russia invaded more than four and a half years ago. It has repeatedly touted the effectiveness of its domestically produced drones, including naval drones deployed throughout the war to hit Russian ships and infrastructure in the Black Sea.
In 2024, the Ukrainian general staff announced it had destroyed the Russian landing ship Cesar Kunikov with naval drones off the coast of Ukraine’s peninsula of Crimea, which was annexed by Russia in 2014.
Ukraine has also claimed to have attacked Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet – believed to carry Russian oil to circumvent sanctions – including in the Mediterranean last December. In March, a Russian liquefied natural gas carrier sank off the Libyan coast following an attack that Putin blamed on Ukraine.
Jalel Harchaoui, a Libya analyst at the Royal United Services Institute, said Ukraine’s strikes in the Mediterranean “were exceptionally brazen and provocative”.
He added: “The question now is how Russia will retaliate,. Perhaps even more pressing is how the [Hafter] family will respond, given how traumatic the scale of the destruction has been for eastern Libyan authorities.”
Additional reporting by Pjotr Sauer

Ukraine shares video of strikes on Russian ships off Libya
Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelensky has shared footage on social media which he says shows strikes on Russian vessels off the coast of Libya on Sunday.

world-e8b12cc5b9.headline: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
world-e8b12cc5b9.fulltext:
What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
- Published
Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.
The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi, co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?
The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.
Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes, has called it "a dangerous escalation".
It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.
Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.
Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.
The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.
And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.
It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".
Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.
Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.
If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?
Impact elsewhere in Europe
As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.
On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders, just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.
This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.
It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.
But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.
Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.
In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.
The three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.
There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.
Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.
Hybrid attacks
Hybrid warfare isn't new but it is on the rise.
It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.
This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.
There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

science-mind-56bbe888f6.headline: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
science-mind-56bbe888f6.fulltext:
A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.
After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels.
The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency.
Advertisement
But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia.
Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates.
Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.”
The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change.
Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”.
Parties also vented their frustration at the hosts, Turkey and Australia, with the joint presidency leading to a sluggish and disjointed negotiating process in the final days of the summit. There was also disquiet from lower-income nations over the lack of new climate finance commitments from richer countries.
Fossil fuel-dependent countries have long sought to delay, obstruct and divert climate talks from making a dent in the worldwide consumption of oil, gas and coal. It was oil-exporting countries that insisted all UN climate decisions should be made by consensus when the COP process was established in 1992, a decision that has hamstrung subsequent meetings by effectively awarding veto power to every nation. Other tactics include delaying talks by raising objections and points of order during meetings and flooding the official agenda with additional discussion areas.
What was new at COP31 was seeing a group like the EU ditching a deal rather than finding a weak compromise in the name of progress, says Joanna Depledge at the University of Cambridge, a seasoned COP observer. “The usual political dynamics were completely upended,” she says of COP31’s endgame. “Usually the EU always backs down at the end. It doesn’t want to be seen as a blocker, but this time it played hardball.”
Many in the climate world are cheering the EU for standing its ground. Bill Hare, the CEO of the influential Climate Analytics think tank, said the deal was “clearly unacceptable”. “The lack of agreement on the main document here shouldn’t be seen as a failure of the COP process, but as a successful defence of the UNFCCC’s integrity against a coordinated attack by a few countries implacably opposed to action on climate change, in particular to any mention of the need to transition away from fossil fuels,” he said in a statement.
But the “no deal” outcome of COP31 is far from good news for those concerned about the world’s direction of travel on climate issues. The global consensus on action is fragmenting, even as climate impacts escalate and the world economy accelerates its embrace of renewable energy and electric technologies. Where does all this leave the COP process?
The debacle underscores the growing scepticism of so-called cover decisions at COPs. With nations at an impasse over even mentioning fossil fuels in any final text, it leaves many wondering what the point of a cover text is at all if it can’t ramp up the ambition signal sent to the rest of the world. Next year’s summit will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and the hosts are highly unlikely to want to risk pushing for a cover decision.
With nations unlikely to agree on bold steps unanimously, the next-best thing is for large groups of countries to forge ahead with real-world change regardless. That means COPs will become more focused on the so-called action agenda, where groups of countries voluntarily band together to make pledges and set out roadmaps for adopting cleaner technologies. Yet whether that can be as powerful as all nations standing together under a singular message of ambition is doubtful.
But despite the disarray of the last fortnight, there are still reasons for hope. Meyer points out that progress was made in other areas of the COP, with 70 countries agreeing to accelerate the electrification of their economies, and countries including Brazil, Denmark and Spain presenting their roadmaps for removing fossil fuels from their economies. “In the real world, there’s a lot of progress,” he says.
The collapse of the negotiations might force better planning and strategy from nations going forward, he suggests. “I think, in a strange kind of way, the breakdown in the negotiations may serve as a wake-up call to the vast majority of countries that want to see progress on climate change,” he says.
There is also a clear signal from the wider economy that change is already under way. Renewables continue to grow faster than analyst predictions at every turn, while electric vehicles are hitting adoption tipping points in growing numbers of countries. The Iran conflict has underscored to many governments the security benefits of home-grown power over fossil fuel imports, with solar and nuclear energy the biggest beneficiaries, the International Energy Agency reported last week. Decarbonisation isn’t happening anywhere near fast enough, but the direction of travel is unmistakable.
UN climate summits have been teetering for many years, with the appearance of consensus maintained thanks to delicately constructed phrases and back-room horse trading. COP31 has brought the disputes and distrust out into the open in a spectacular fashion. Perhaps, out of the flames of this summit, a more honest and realistic approach to climate diplomacy can emerge.

ai-81a464b2bd.headline: Trump reportedly called into Nvidia board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return
ai-81a464b2bd.fulltext:
A close ally of Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, President Donald Trump reportedly dialed into an Nvidia board meeting to push for the ousted CEO’s return, Semafor reported on Monday. Trump got his way, as Nvidia announced Huang’s reinstatement shortly afterward.
“I spoke to them, let me put it that way … And I convinced them,” the president told CNBC.
Huang was forced to step down from his role as CEO, which he held for 33 years, after news broke that he had affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees, including a direct report.
“President Trump was totally involved and this is a great decision by the NVIDIA board. We have to protect our geniuses,” White House communications director Steven Cheung told Semafor.
The president took to his social media app, Truth Social, to remark that “the United States government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security.”
According to Nvidia’s press release about Huang’s reinstatement as CEO and president, the company claimed that “the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”
While Trump has declared that Huang “did absolutely nothing wrong,” many government officials aren’t buying the president’s point of view. Huang is still expected to testify in closed-door conversations with three committees of the House of Representatives on December 1. He is also slated to appear before the Senate Banking Committee to testify publicly, though that hearing has not been scheduled yet.
“People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it’s a threat to lose him,” Trump said to CNBC.
Trump has maintained this position through the scandal, even denying that he was ever told about Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang (no relation). The New York Times reported, on the contrary, that Trump’s secretary of state and national security adviser Marco Rubio briefed him aboard Air Force One in May.
Earlier this spring, Rubio also supervised the drafting of a memo that circulated among top policymakers, warning that Alice Huang was spying for China’s Ministry of State Security.

ai-aa93777566.headline: Trump endorses Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia, says US has no evidence of wrongdoing
ai-aa93777566.fulltext:
President Trump praised Nvidia’s decision on Monday to reinstate founder Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO and president, saying on his social network Truth Social that “the United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.”
The Nvidia board’s statement had also referred to consultations with “senior levels of the United States government” as informing its decision. It said that, based on that input, Mr. Huang’s reinstatement was deemed not a national security risk.
In his comments on Monday, Trump claimed that U.S. Attorney General [Todd Blanche] had found no evidence that Mr. Huang had engaged in unlawful conduct. It’s an unusual statement for a U.S. president to make, as the attorney general typically conducts those investigations independently. Notably, Attorney General Blanche has not yet made a formal statement on the case.
There’s also indication that President Trump may have been aware of the decision before the announcement by the Nvidia board. Speaking to a PBS journalist over the weekend, he said of Huang “he’s back where he should be and we see he did absolutely nothing wrong.” Asked to clarify about whether he meant Huang would be reinstated, Trump said, “I hope so, I hope so.”
Huang was accused of having multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a direct report at Nvidia and another unnamed employee. However, the affair of most concern was the one with the alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (no relation). Ms. Huang was an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed, which had purchased billions in Nvidia chips over the past couple of years. This relationship had raised national security concerns about whether the CEO ties to Ms. Huang could have compromised sensitive information or facilitated China’s access to advanced U.S. AI chips, which are subject to export restrictions.
Trump said last week that he believed this relationship didn’t threaten the U.S.’s national security, and instead said that no one had proven she’s a spy. “She may not be a spy,” the president said, adding that “China plays games with us, and we play games with China.”
Trump’s full statement on Huang’s return, released on Monday, is below.
The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen’s return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security. The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct. On a personal note, I have gotten to know Jensen, and he is a Great Patriot and National Treasure. Separately, NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company’s compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security. Congratulations to Jensen, the NVIDIA Board, to the People of the United States — and, indeed, the World! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP

Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive, "effective immediately," the US tech giant said in a statement on Monday, in a surprising U-turn that sent shares soaring.
Nvidia's board of directors unanimously voted to reinstate Huang, 63, following discussions and meetings with him, as well as receiving input from "senior levels" of the US government, the chipmaker said. He was also resuming his role as director of the board.
The company's chips have become a key technology for training and running artificial intelligence. Concerns that Nvidia might be less successful without Huang not only caused the company's share price to fall following his resignation, but also weighed on the market as a whole.
The US economy is also heavily dependent on investment in artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Huang was feted by staff at Nvidia's headquarters following his reappointment, as shown in a video broadcast by CNBC. He expressed his gratitude for "second chances" and vowed to be a better boss the second time round.
Announcement sparks broad US stock market rally
Huang's surprise return sparked a strong recovery on US stock markets. The Nasdaq 100 closed up 6.86% at 26,746.10 points. However, the index had fallen about 16% between the end of October, when the New York Times first reported on an alleged Chinese espionage operation involving the Nvidia chief, and the end of last week.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, which also includes Nvidia shares, gained 3.01% to 49,595.31 points on Monday. The benchmark index had also suffered heavy losses in recent weeks. The broader S&P 500, which had likewise come under pressure, rose 4.73% to 7,237.17 points.
Nvidia shares surged by almost a third to around $165, recovering about $950 billion in market value. This recouped a substantial portion of the losses suffered since the end of October. However, the stock remained about 23% below its closing level of just over $215 on October 28.
Huang's return could help restore lost confidence in the AI sector and provide some direction to volatile markets, at least temporarily, according to market analyst Timo Emden of CapTrader. He described the move as a calming influence on markets caught between enthusiasm for AI, concerns about interest rates and profit-taking.
Trump welcomes 'correct' decision
Minutes after the statement was published, US President Donald Trump welcomed what he called the "correct and proper decision," in a post on Truth Social, adding that the US government "has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk to national security."

Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its CEO, president and board director with immediate effect, after the company determined following input from US officials that the move would not pose a national security risk.
Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive after Donald Trump directly intervened with the US AI chipmaker’s board of directors, in a stunning reversal of the tech billionaire’s downfall.
Speaking on Monday shortly after Nvidia’s surprise announcement that Huang had been restored to the top job – less than two weeks after he resigned – Trump said that he had “convinced” the board to do it. “I made the deal,” he told CNBC. Huang had resigned after reports of extramarital affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy and two Nvidia employees.
“It’s very exciting news. I felt very strongly that he should come back,” the US president said.
Huang said he was “honored to return to Nvidia” and lead “one of the most consequential technology companies in the world”. He added: “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.”
Nvidia shares surged on the news of Huang’s return, jumping 32% and adding more than $1tn (£760bn) to the company’s market value in New York on Monday, while Trump, who had persistently called for Huang’s return, said: “The country needs Jensen’s leadership.”
The chipmaker’s move to bring Huang back marks a sharp reversal from its board’s decision days earlier to rule out his return. The US vice-president, JD Vance, played a key role in discussions between the White House, Huang and Nvidia, according to the New York Times.
The US government has been investigating Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company formerly run by Huang’s alleged former lover, Alice Huang (no relation), over suspected diversion of semiconductors in breach of export controls, amid concerns Nvidia’s powerful AI chips may have been smuggled to China. Alice Huang has also been named in multiple reports as a Chinese spy.
The same day as Huang’s reinstatement, the US government announced it had added Megaspeed to a federal trade blacklist, preventing US companies from selling chips or other advanced technology to the Singaporean business.
Trump said on Monday the US government had no “evidence that [Jensen Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct” and that the attorney general, Todd Blanche, felt Huang was “exonerated”.
The US president told CNBC the US had to “protect our geniuses”, adding that the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, praised Huang at last week’s Apec summit in Shenzhen. Adding that he had talked to Nvidia’s directors, he said: “I’ve been speaking to the [Nvidia] board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it. I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company.”
Nvidia’s share price had fallen by a quarter in the days after Huang resigned on 12 November. The falls were mirrored by a wider AI rout in global stock markets last week as investors feared new leadership at Nvidia could dampen prospects for AI companies that rely on the company’s chips to develop and operate AI tools such as chatbots, as well as having close financial ties with the chipmaker.
News of his shock reinstatement sparked a wider rally not just in Nvidia’s shares but on Wall Street as a whole, sending the Nasdaq composite index up 6.5% and the S&P 500 by 4.7%. The US dollar was lifted to a 19-month high.
In a statement, Nvidia said its board of directors had talked to Huang and were “satisfied with respect to Mr Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia”. Nvidia added that it had received input from “senior levels” of the US government and was confident his reinstatement “poses no national security risk”.
A senior Democrat, Elizabeth Warren, a senator for Massachusetts, said the decision was “reckless”, adding that it did not change the fact that Huang owed Congress answers about Nvidia’s compliance with trade restrictions on its powerful AI chips. He is due to give evidence to Congress on 1 December. The state of California is also investigating if Nvidia’s advanced chips ended up in China in violation of US restrictions.
She said his return increased the urgency of Congress passing export control bills “and making sure that Nvidia does not lobby to kill that legislation and put our national security at risk”.
Nvidia said an independent investigation into allegations Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation was ongoing and “will proceed to conclusion”.
Harvey Jones, the Nvidia chair, who was appointed this month after Huang’s resignation, said: “The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers.”
Huang built Nvidia from a video-game chip designer into the dominant supplier of AI processors, steering its roadmap, customer deals and Washington ties along the way. He resigned after revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, whom US authorities suspect of spying for China, an allegation Beijing denies. It was also reported that Huang had an intimate relationship with two other Nvidia employees.
Trump praised Nvidia’s board for making “the correct and proper decision” and said: “The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy.”
It came hours after reports that Alice Huang had been in contact with an official in China’s spy agency while she was having an affair with the Nvidia boss. People with knowledge of US intelligence reports claimed she was in touch with the Chinese official until this autumn, according to the New York Times.
The Arm Holdings chief executive, Rene Haas, who had been approached to succeed Huang, has signed a new deal that will keep him in his current role until 2033. Huang had been replaced on a temporary basis by Colette Kress, Nvidia’s finance chief.
Elon Musk, who had called for Huang to return in an open letter backed by other Silicon Valley heavyweights, posted on X: “Welcome back the main man,” alongside a picture of him shaking hands with Huang. Trump said he had spoken to Musk “over the last week or so” about the Huang situation.
Sam North, a market analyst at the trading platform eToro, said: “Jensen Huang’s return underlines how much of the AI trade still rests on one man.”
Huang’s reinstatement has echoes of another recent real-life Silicon Valley drama. His return has taken place almost three years to the day since OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, brought back its chief executive, Sam Altman, after a similar bout of turmoil. Altman was removed by his board on 17 November 2023 but was restored five days later following an internal power battle.
In a post on X on Monday Altman wrote: “Jensen!”
