Updated - November 24, 2026  at 05:50 AM.
| 
         Washington
     President Donald Trump saw little choice but to fight to reinstate Jensen Huang at AI behemoth Nvidia.
The president has staked the nation's economic growth on artificial intelligence, and worried Huang's ouster was not only tanking the stock market -- but also risked putting the US behind Beijing in the race for dominance in the field if Huang, widely seen by backers and critics as a generational talent in artificial intelligence, were to be poached by a Chinese firm.
And the president, a thrice-married man and real estate maven who has seen his own marital infidelity scrutinised in the press, bristled at Huang being ousted from the company he built because of extramarital affairs, including one with an executive at a Singapore-based company who US officials suspect was a Chinese spy.
So Trump engaged in an extraordinary level of behind-the-scenes manoeuvring to reinstate Huang, starting almost immediately after the CEO's fall from grace when he resigned on Nov. 12 as reports trickled out about a trio of affairs.
The president stated plainly in a CNBC interview on Monday that he used his considerable sway to get Huang his job back. “I spoke to them,” Trump said of the company's board of directors. “Let me just put it that way. And I convinced them.”
Monday's reinstatement was a remarkable turnaround by Nvidia's board, which had insisted days after Huang's ouster that it was not considering such a move, even as Trump pushed for it and thousands signed an online petition calling for Huang's return.
Trump stayed loyal to the iconic CEO who was a trusted adviser to the White House on artificial intelligence and a big donor to the president's ballroom project, arguing the company and America would be best served with Huang in charge of Nvidia.
Trump is also a big personal believer and investor in Nvidia, a leader in the global artificial intelligence industry's boom. At the end of 2025, he had Nvidia holdings worth between USD 12.5 million and USD 58 million, according to his annual financial disclosure report filed in June 2026. That's up from USD 615,000 to USD 1.3 million in Nvidia stock in his disclosed holdings at the end of 2024.
The White House has said the president's portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions. “All holdings are maintained in discretionary accounts and invested through computer-based model portfolios that automatically replicate recognised indexes,” said Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman. “Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold.”
Trump said that the walloping AI stocks had taken following Huang's sacking helped him make his case. Some of his closest advisers helped persuade the board: Vice President JD Vance, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who as recently as last week had called for a “dramatic shake-up” at Nvidia.
Huang is far from the first CEO to fall from grace because of infidelity or inappropriate relationships. In recent years, prominent executives like McDonald's Steve Easterbrook, BP's Bernard Looney and Intel's Brian Krzanich were forced out of their jobs.
Trump downplayed the issue. “He's apologised for that to the company, to the country and to his family and his wife, who's a fantastic person,” Trump said on CNBC. “People are realising the job he's done.”
Huang's scandal had additional complexity because one of the extramarital relationships was with a woman who US officials suspect had been an asset of China's intelligence service. Beijing has denied it.
As part of his campaign for Huang's reinstatement, Trump said US officials assured the company that Huang -- who acknowledged his relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang -- did not present a national security risk.
Trump said that the Nvidia situation was different from other corporate scandals because Huang is an unprecedented talent who is shaping a technology that could impact just about every facet of life in the years to come. Trump also said he was concerned Huang could have been scooped up by a Chinese firm.
“This is different because of the vast amount of knowledge in his brain,” Trump said.
Vance stepped up his involvement over the weekend in making Trump's case to the Nvidia board, according to a person familiar with the matter.
The person, who was not authorised to comment publicly and spoke on the condition of anonymity, said that the White House deemed Vance, who worked in Silicon Valley before jumping into politics, to have the stature to serve as an effective emissary in helping Nvidia board members overcome their reservations.
Trump marvelled during his CNBC interview at the impact Huang's reinstatement had on the stock market. The S&P 500 leapt 4.7 per cent on Monday following Huang's return.
During his time in the White House, the president has looked at the market as the ultimate validator of his leadership. The ebbs and flows of the market have shaped some of his most significant policies, including decisions on his ongoing war against Iran as well as his administration's tariff policy.
Trump views the AI build-out as a key driver of the economy. The biggest tech firms have spent roughly USD 800 billion this year building data centres and cramming them with the latest semiconductors from Nvidia as well as computing equipment, electrical components, HVAC gear, and copper wiring.
The investment is projected to only grow in coming years, and could total USD 10.3 trillion from 2025 through 2032, equal to about 3.6 per cent of the nation's economy, according to research from Columbia University economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh.
All the while, Trump has urged local communities to accept new data centres, even as political opposition to them has mounted. The surge in data centre construction has lifted wages for skilled workers such as electricians and plumbers, who are in short supply. And the demand for semiconductors is so voracious that it has increased the cost of gaming stations, smartphones, and laptops, worsening inflation.
The AI explosion has also significantly enriched American investors, particularly the wealthiest one-tenth of US families who own roughly 85 per cent of stock wealth. The AI-fueled jump has fattened Americans' 401(k)s and boosted consumer spending enough to accelerate the economy's expansion, leading some economists to worry in the wake of Huang's initial departure that if the stock market had kept tumbling, growth could slow.
For a Republican, Trump has long taken a surprisingly interventionist role in the private sector, snapping up government stakes in companies like Intel, US Steel, Westinghouse, and a long list of smaller but important rare earths interests. In an earlier deal with Nvidia, he secured 15 per cent of the company's revenues from sales of older chips to China.
Those deals have attracted some scrutiny from lawmakers. But Trump's role in getting Huang's job back drew immediate bipartisan fire.
Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a longtime ally of Trump, wrote on X that there was “something profoundly wrong” about Huang's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy and questioned the wisdom of returning him to run the most advanced chipmaking company in the world.
Meanwhile, Sen. Tim Scott, R-S.C., announced Monday that Huang will testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who are expected to assume leadership of their chambers in January, criticised the decision to reinstate Huang, with Jeffries in a statement calling it “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.”
Nevertheless, Trump said the scandal that shook one of the world's most valuable companies and caused ripples in the global economy could, in the end, be “a net positive” for Huang and the broader AI industry.
“It was a terrible spotlight in one way,” Trump argued. “But in another way, it's shown how advanced this company is. How incredibly advanced it is with respect to him."

Trump faces backlash after saying he 'convinced' Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang
- Published
Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over a reported affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
The company came under pressure by Donald Trump to reappoint Huang - and on Monday, the US president said he "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring him back.
But now both Trump and Nvidia are facing bipartisan backlash from lawmakers, just as Huang is due to testify before Congress next week.
The CEO's comeback helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that left the S&P 500 in correction territory, and added nearly $1 trillion to Nvidia's market value.
Stock prices for Nvidia fell sharply after Huang stepped down, but jumped by 31% after he was reappointed on Monday - adding about $1tn to the company's market value.
But Nvidia's closing price was still down slightly from its Friday morning opening price.
As Asian stock markets opened, Nvidia racked up more gains and helped lift other share prices across the tech sector.
Board Chairman Harvey C Jones said in a statement earlier in the day: "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.
It was only last Tuesday that the board explicitly said it did not intend to reinstate him.
Huang resigned from Nvidia on 12 November following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman, Alice Huang, who was alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.
On Monday, the US Commerce Department announced it was preparing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singapore-based Nvidia customer where Alice Huang was CEO.
In a brief interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said he had spoken to Nvidia's board of directors and "convinced" them to bring back Huang. Trump praised the Nvidia board for acting "really responsibly" in reinstating the CEO.
"They did ask for assurance on the national security threat," Trump said. "And we gave them assurances at least with everything we know. And we know a lot."
"People say, is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the president added.
The president was asked whether Nvidia stock losses after Huang resigned last week had influenced his decision to personally intervene.
"Probably so," Trump said.

  - Published13 hours ago
- How important are Nvidia and Jensen Huang to the US economy? 
  - Published13 hours ago
Congress vows to investigate Nvidia and the Trump administration's role
The head of the International Association for Safe and Ethical AI told the BBC that the Nvidia board must have been under "enormous pressure" from the White House to reinstate Huang.
Prof Stuart Russell, who is professor of computer science at UC Berkeley, said the stock price of Nvidia and similar firms has been a major factor in "underpinning US economic growth for years".
"I assume the White House was worried that the markets would go down a lot further in the next few weeks unless they go him back in," he says.
Trump's vocal backing of Huang comes despite the concerns of US lawmakers, including some Republicans, over the CEO's affair and Nvidia's compliance with US export controls.
Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to lead the House of Representatives as Speaker when Democrats take control in January called the decision to reinstate Huang "indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible" and vowed that Congress will conduct "a swift, thorough and wide-ranging investigation".
"We will not allow America's national security to be sold out by the Trump Administration for personal financial gain," he said, echoing many lawmakers on Monday who said that Congress must pass strong export control legislation.
Huang is scheduled to appear before Congress for a closed-door interview with three House committees on 1 December. Two days later, he has been asked to testify before the Senate banking committee.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, who is set to be chairwoman of the Senate Banking Committee once Democrats take control of the chamber in January, said in a statement that the reinstatement was "reckless".
"The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement," she also said.
Republicans, too, called for answers.
"Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang," said Republican Representative Don Bacon, who chairs a House subcommittee on cyber security.
"We cannot say we want to win the AI race and then give China our best technology. We need sunlight on who is responsible."
The chair of the Senate's select committee on intelligence, Republican Tom Cotton said: "The controversy with Nvidia and Megaspeed is just the tip of the iceberg, and it's not resolved because Jensen Huang has his job back."

Trump's personal Nvidia investments
Since returning last year to the White House, Trump has amassed a significant level of investment in Nvidia. Recent financial disclosures show he purchased $265,000 in its stock and sold as much as $15,000 worth of shares in September.
A BBC review of his government financial disclosures for the last two years shows he purchased shares of Nvidia stock worth between $23m and $86m (£18m and £66m). And he has bought Nvidia stock 85 separate times through a number of investment accounts.
The value of those holdings would have been affected by the recent fall in Nvidia's stock price amid Huang's exit.
Trump has also sold some of his stake in Nvidia since returning to the presidency. Over 19 sales, Trump gained between $3.5m and $10.2m, according to his government disclosures.
The BBC has contacted the White House.
Both Trump and White House have repeatedly rejected assertions that he has profited from the presidency. The president has said "everybody" was making money from rising stocks and he does not make decisions related to his investment accounts.
The White House has emphasised that Trump has placed his businesses in a trust managed by his sons.

Anthropic launches Claude Ship to review, fix and approve code changes
Anthropic's new Claude Ship brings AI agents to GitHub that can automatically review, fix, and even approve routine code changes based on a team's rules, helping developers ship software much faster.
Artificial intelligence has been helping software engineers write code for a while now, and Anthropic is ready to hand over the next big part of the job. On Monday, the newly public AI company launched Claude Ship, a new set of AI agents designed to automatically review, fix, and even approve routine code changes before they go live.
While several AI coding tools already scan code for errors, Claude Ship goes a step further. Instead of just flagging mistakes and waiting for a programmer to step in, it allows an AI agent to actually sign off on code updates based on rules set by a company’s engineering team.
Why Anthropic built Claude Ship
Over the past year, AI coding assistants have become very good at generating large volumes of code quickly. However, that speed has created a new headache for tech teams. Even when AI writes the code in minutes, human developers still have to spend hours checking every proposed update, known as a pull request, before approving it.
In a blog post explaining the launch, Anthropic pointed out that having a human approve every single change works well when people are writing every line of code. Today, many developers rely heavily on AI agents to build software.
Anthropic noted that on its own Claude Code team, Claude already writes most of the code, and the company wanted every step after a pull request to move just as fast. Claude Ship is built to clear that bottleneck.
How Claude Ship works
Claude Ship brings together three different tools to manage the journey from a code submission to a final approval. The first is Code Review, which is already generally available and scans proposed code changes to catch bugs and other issues.
Joining it are two new AI agents that are launching in beta. The first is PR Steward, which actively fixes problems rather than just listing them. It handles common roadblocks such as failing automated tests, known as CI checks, merge conflicts, and feedback flagged by Code Review. To keep things transparent, PR Steward leaves a comment after every update explaining exactly what it changed and how developers can undo it if anything goes wrong.
The second new agent, Claude Approvals, is the biggest shift in the workflow. It decides whether a code change is safe to approve by following an approval policy written by the development team in plain, natural language and saved as a file inside the project repository. The agent weighs signals like Code Review findings and Anthropic’s own classifiers against those rules before giving the green light.
Keeping human developers in control
Handing approval powers to an AI naturally raises concerns about a faulty update slipping through and breaking live software. Anthropic says it has built several guardrails so teams do not lose control of their codebases.
Because the new agents are still in beta, Anthropic recommends that teams run Claude Approvals in an observe-only mode at first to see how it behaves before letting it make real decisions. Companies can also start small by testing it on just one repository and setting monthly spending limits.
Developers remain in charge of where Claude Ship runs, how deeply it inspects code through Quick, Standard, or Deep settings, and which critical changes must always be sent to a human for the final call.
Availability and rollout
Claude Ship is rolling out for repositories hosted on GitHub and is available to users on Anthropic’s Claude Team and Enterprise plans. While Code Review is already widely available, both PR Steward and Claude Approvals are currently being offered in beta for early adopters looking to speed up how quickly their software gets shipped.

India AI funding nearly doubles to $1.6B in Jan-Sept 2026: Tracxn
Early-stage funding led the investment mix. Mumbai overtook Bengaluru to become the city with the largest funding during the period.
India AI companies raised $1.6 billion in equity funding in the first nine months of 2026, nearly double the level in the year-ago period, according to a report by Tracxn Technologies.
This, in fact, is the highest funding grosser across the nine-month periods covered since 2019.
"India AI companies raised $1.6 billion in equity funding in nine months 2026, up 96% from $822 million in nine months 2025 and 162% from $616 million in nine months 2024, marking the highest funding total across the nine-month periods covered since 2019," the report by data intelligence platform Tracxn Technologies' said.
According to the 'India AI - 9M 2026' report, the funding was raised across 87 rounds, compared to 149 rounds during the year-ago period. This indicates that the increase was driven by a relatively small number of large deals.
Early-stage funding led the investment mix. Mumbai overtook Bengaluru to become the city with the largest funding during the period.
The ten largest rounds in 2026 raised $1.5 billion, 90% of the $1.6 billion total.
Neysa, a Mumbai-based AI cloud provider, raised the largest chunk, a $600 million Series B in February, equivalent to 37% of all funding. Sarvam, the Bengaluru-based generative AI developer, raised $255 million in a Series B in June and a further $90.4 million in August. Yotta raised $150 million in July.
"Series A and later rounds fell 33% to 24 from 36, and first-time funded companies fell 60% to 24 from 60," the report said.
Globally, AI companies raised $383.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026; India's $1.6 billion was 0.4% of that, ninth among countries.
Early-stage funding rose 191% to $1.3 billion between January and September, up from $434 million in the year-ago period. Early-stage rounds fell 38% to 21. The average early-stage round was $60.2 million against $12.8 million in the year-ago period.
According to the report, 111 investors backed India AI companies in the first nine months of 2026, down from 169 in the year-ago period. First-time investors fell to 43, and international investors fell to 29.
Peak XV Partners led early-stage investors with three investments, followed by Prosus and Khosla Ventures with two each. Antler, IvyCap Ventures and Finvolve made two seed investments each, while SoftBank Vision Fund and Creaegis backed one late-stage round each.

world-e9a9b97263.headline: US adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist as Nvidia’s Huang returns as CEO
world-e9a9b97263.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera

US adds Megaspeed to trade blacklist as Nvidia’s Huang returns as CEO
Bureau of Industry and Security adds Singapore-based firm involved in Nvidia spy scandal to export control list.
The United States has added the Singapore-based company at the centre of an alleged spying scandal involving Nvidia to its trade blacklist.
The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) placed Megaspeed International and six other firms in Southeast Asia on its Entity List on Monday, hours after Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia as CEO in a stunning comeback that sent tech stocks soaring.
Megaspeed and the other entities were determined to be “acting contrary to the national security or foreign policy interests of the United States”, BIS, which sits under the US Department of Commerce, said in a filing to the Federal Register.
The designations mean that anyone seeking to ship the entities advanced US technology, including Nvidia’s top-end graphics processing units (GPUs) used in AI, must obtain an export licence.
Megaspeed’s blacklisting comes as divisions in US President Donald Trump’s administration over China’s access to Nvidia chips have been laid bare in recent weeks amid claims Huang was romantically involved with a woman accused of working with Chinese intelligence.
While US officials have been scrutinising Megaspeed’s compliance with export controls for years, US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s department had declined to place the company on its trade blacklist, prompting recriminations from administration officials known to hold more hawkish views on China, including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
Trump felt ‘very strongly’
Trump on Monday played down the national security concerns around Nvidia as he confirmed that he had personally intervened with the company’s board of directors to push for Huang’s reinstatement.
Trump, who has cultivated a close relationship with the top Nvidia executive during his second term, told CNBC that he felt “very strongly” about Huang’s role at the chip giant and that he offered the board assurances about risks to national security.
Shaoyu Yuan, a visiting assistant professor at New York University’s Center for Global Affairs who specialises in security issues, said Trump’s intervention was the latest example of the president making policy based on personal rapport rather than a “consistent security standard”.
“The incoherence is in the wider policy. Washington blacklists a middleman for moving Nvidia chips to China while it licenses Nvidia to sell H200 chips to China directly and takes a 25 percent cut,” Yuan told Al Jazeera, referring to the Trump administration’s announcement last year that it would allow the sale of some Nvidia GPUs to China in exchange for the company handing over a portion of the revenues to the government.
“Treasury Secretary Bessent has said other departments wanted this listing for months, and Commerce acted only after the scandal became public.”
US officials have accused Megaspeed International’s former top executive Alice Huang of working with China’s Ministry of State Security in an intelligence-gathering operation targeting Huang.
Beijing has rejected the claims as “groundless speculation” and “an attempt to smear and malign China”. Alice Huang has not publicly commented on the claims, which are based on US intelligence first reported by The New York Times and the Financial Times.
Nvidia shares skyrocketed 31.5 percent following the news of Huang’s reinstatement, helping the US stock market achieve its strongest single-day performance in more than 18 months.
The benchmark S&P 500 closed up 4.7 percent, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite jumped 6.51 percent.
The rally continued in Asia on Tuesday, with key indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan roaring back after a punishing sell-off the previous day.
Taiwan’s Taiex led the gains, surging 9.1 percent as of 04:15 GMT.
Japan’s Nikkei 225 was up 4 percent, while South Korea’s Kospi was 7 percent higher.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng Index was 0.4 percent in the red.
Concerns ‘serious, unresolved’
Apart from Megaspeed International, the expanded blacklist announced on Monday identifies three firms said to be based in Malaysia, two in Singapore and one in Thailand.
BIS named the entities as MSFusion, PT Megaspeed International, Speedmatrix, Apex Enterprise Solutions, Swiftdata and Megaspeed (Thailand).
Malaysia’s Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry said in a statement that, based on official records, PT Megaspeed International is not a Malaysian entity.
The ministry said authorities would inform all data centre operators in Malaysia of the expanded blacklist and advise them against hosting or providing services to the designated firms.
“Malaysia remains committed to a secure, transparent and rules-based trading environment and will not allow itself to be used as a channel to circumvent export controls. Action will be taken against parties found to have contravened any laws,” the ministry said.
Singapore’s Ministry of Digital Development and Information and Thailand’s Ministry of Industry did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Speaking during a visit to Australia on Tuesday, Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said the city-state did not want to be “used and abused” by companies seeking to circumvent US export controls.
Megaspeed International, which is under investigation by the US Department of Justice on suspicion of diverting high-end chips to China in violation of export controls, did not respond to a request for comment.
The Singapore-based data centre company has previously insisted that it is a “legitimate and lawful business” and that media reports about its operations contained claims that were “not supported by verifiable evidence”.
Shiva Rajgopal, a professor of accounting at Columbia Business School, said it was “extraordinary” that the Trump administration had decided to blacklist Megaspeed while also pushing for Huang’s reinstatement.
“The board reinstated its CEO before the investigations into Megaspeed and his ties to it have concluded. Today’s listing shows those concerns are serious and unresolved,” Rajgopal told Al Jazeera.
“For the chip industry, the lesson is that knowing your customer is now a board-level issue,” Rajgopal said.

Deep-tech company olee.space has secured a contract from the Defence Research & Development Organisation (DRDO), Ministry of Defence, to develop an indigenous laser-link communication system for drones. The system will enable secure, high-speed, two-way data transmission between ground stations and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in flight.
The project will involve the design and development of ground-based and airborne Free Space Optical Communication (FSOC) terminals, incorporating automatic Pointing, Acquisition and Tracking (PAT) technology. The system is expected to be developed within 18 months and will comprise a tripod-mounted ground terminal and a compact optical payload integrated with the drone.
Laser communication technology uses beams of light to transmit data through the atmosphere, offering an alternative to conventional radio-frequency communication. Unlike radio-based systems, optical links are less susceptible to electronic jamming and can provide high data transmission speeds over long line-of-sight distances.
The technology has gained attention in military applications, particularly in conflict zones where electronic warfare and radio-frequency interference can disrupt drone communications. Fibre-optic tethered drones have been used to overcome radio jamming, although their operational range and mobility are restricted by the physical cable. Laser-based communication offers a cable-free alternative while maintaining a secure communication link.
The system being developed by olee.space will enable full-duplex communication, allowing simultaneous transmission and reception of data between the drone and the ground station. Automatic tracking technology will maintain the optical connection as the drone moves during flight.
James, Co-founder of olee.space, said, “Holding a laser link on a moving drone is one of the hardest problems in communications, and olee.space is one of very few companies globally working on this capability. We launched this programme a year ago, and we’re proud to have DRDO’s trust. This is Aatmanirbhar Bharat in action: frontier technology, built in India, competing with the world.” The contract adds to India’s efforts to develop indigenous defence communication technologies for unmanned platforms and reduce dependence on imported systems.
olee.space is a Pune-based deep-tech company developing laser communication systems for defence, aerospace and critical infrastructure applications. The company undertakes optical design, system development and field testing in-house, focusing on secure communication technologies for applications on the ground, in the air and in space.

BENGALURU: A startup, olee.space, has secured a contract from the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) to develop an indigenous laser-link communication system for drones, a technology that could help address one of the major vulnerabilities exposed in modern warfare: the disruption of communication through radio-frequency jamming.
The system will use beams of light to transmit data between a ground station and a drone in flight, eliminating the need for conventional radio links or physical cables. It is designed to provide secure, high-speed, two-way communication over long distances, provided there is a clear line of sight.
The vulnerability of radio-based drone communication has become particularly evident in the Russia-Ukraine war, where electronic warfare and radio jamming have disrupted drone operations. In response, some drones have been deployed with fibre-optic cables trailing behind them. Since these cables carry data through physical connections, they cannot be disrupted through radio-frequency jamming. However, they restrict the drone's range and can get entangled, damaged or severed during operations.
Laser-based communication seeks to offer a similar advantage without the physical tether. Data is transmitted through a narrow beam of light, making the link resistant to radio-frequency interference and difficult to intercept.
Under the contract, olee.space will design and develop complete ground and airborne Free Space Optical Communication (FSOC) terminals, incorporating an automatic Pointing, Acquisition and Tracking (PAT) system. The ground terminal will be mounted on a tripod, while a compact optical payload will be integrated into the drone. The system will support full-duplex communication, allowing data to be transmitted simultaneously in both directions.
One of the key engineering challenges is maintaining a stable laser connection with a drone that is constantly moving. The PAT system will automatically locate, acquire and track the airborne terminal to keep the communication link aligned during flight.
The company has been given 18 months to develop the system, including both ground and airborne components.
James, co-founder of olee.space, said maintaining a laser link with a moving drone was among the most challenging problems in communications. The company began work on the programme a year ago and sees the DRDO contract as an opportunity to develop the capability indigenously.
olee.space develops laser communication systems for defence, aerospace and critical infrastructure. Its work spans optical design, system development and field trials.
The contract is part of the broader push to develop indigenous technologies for defence applications, particularly in areas where secure and uninterrupted communication is critical to unmanned aerial operations.

india-3284f2fcaa.headline: Invoking Bengal famine, India tells UNSC costs of conflict not shared equally
india-3284f2fcaa.fulltext:
India has invoked the 1943 Bengal famine at the UN Security Council to highlight the disproportionate impact of conflicts on the Global South, calling for measures to prevent food insecurity amid the Ukraine war.
India’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Harish Parvathaneni, told a high-level briefing of the Security Council on Monday that developing countries were bearing the brunt of food, fuel, fertiliser and energy shortages caused by global conflicts.
“India has consistently emphasised that the costs of conflict are not shared equally,” he said.
“Global South countries are the most adversely affected by the food, fuel, and fertiliser crisis caused by today’s global conflicts,” he added.
Invoking the Bengal famine, which killed over three million people, Parvathaneni said it was a reminder of the “terrible human cost” of a distant conflict caused by unchecked wartime priorities and calculations.
Addressing the briefing on ‘Protecting critical energy infrastructure and Black Sea lifelines of global food supply’, Parvathaneni said that in an interconnected world, the implications of the Ukraine conflict, now in its fifth year, were being felt everywhere.
Recalling Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s message that the world has to move from endless war to the end of war, he reiterated India’s readiness to contribute to all efforts towards a peaceful resolution of the conflict.
He also stressed that Modi was firmly on the side of the Global South when he said that “this is not an era of war.”
India noted with concern that conflicts exacerbate food insecurity by disrupting agriculture, displacing communities, damaging infrastructure and hindering humanitarian access.
Their consequences extend globally through disruptions to energy, fertiliser supplies, transport and agricultural trade, disproportionately affecting the Global South.
“For the Global South, peace is not in the abstract. It is achieved when hungry mouths are fed, when a ship reaches a port, and when a seafarer returns home safe,” Parvathaneni said.
India called on the Security Council to prioritise humanitarian access, protection of civilian infrastructure and freedom of navigation, ensuring that humanitarian supplies and legitimate trade remain unaffected.
“For India, this is why dialogue and diplomacy, safe commercial shipping and uninterrupted grain and energy flows are practical necessities,” he said.
“This current situation is not different from the time of the Second World War, when peoples not responsible for the start of the conflict became their unintended collateral damage,” he added.
“The pain and suffering caused by the devastating Bengal famine of 1943 in India that killed over 3 million people in India, is a stark reminder of the terrible human cost of a distant conflict caused by unchecked wartime priorities and calculations,” Parvathaneni said.
“It is precisely because of these harsh consequences that India attaches such importance to preventing food insecurity,” he said.
Parvathaneni said India’s commitment to protecting Black Sea lifelines and global food supplies was rooted in the recognition that the region, like India, was one of the world’s major food baskets.
He noted that the Black Sea region and India together account for nearly a fifth of global cereal production, while Russia and Ukraine account for almost a quarter of global exports of wheat, maize and barley.
“Their importance to global food security underscores how disruptions to agricultural production, maritime connectivity, and international trade can have consequences far beyond the immediate regions affected,” he said.
He highlighted India’s humanitarian assistance, including wheat supplies to Afghanistan, rice to Sudan and aid to Palestine, as an example of its commitment to global food supply chains.
India also expressed concern over merchant vessels and their crews increasingly coming under attack in global conflicts, citing incidents in which Indian seafarers had lost their lives.
“We call for an end to the targeting of commercial shipping and seafarers, and for safe navigation through international waterways to be restored at the earliest,” Parvathaneni said.
He recalled that India and Liberia had launched the Group of Friends on Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers during the UN high-level week in September.
UN Under-Secretary-General for Political and Peacebuilding Affairs Rosemary DiCarlo warned that attacks on energy infrastructure were more extensive than during the corresponding period last year, disrupting heating, electricity and water supplies.
She also expressed concern over continued drone attacks in the Black Sea, threatening civilian navigation and disrupting food exports.
World Food Programme (WFP) Executive Director Luke Lindberg, briefing via video conference, warned that Black Sea food shipments had fallen sharply despite grain remaining available.
He said around 10 million tonnes of Russian and Ukrainian wheat, enough to feed 44 million people, may not reach global markets this year.
Lindberg urged member states to rally around three “red lines”: no more famines, no more weaponisation of food and no more attacks on humanitarians.
UN Development Programme (UNDP) Administrator Alexander De Croo said the agency was working with national and local authorities in Ukraine to restore power and essential services ahead of winter, while laying the foundations for longer-term recovery.
(PTI)

work-careers-504d8aee93.headline: India’s white-collar hiring projected to grow 8.16 per cent in 2027

India’s white-collar hiring projected to grow 8.16 per cent in 2027
foundit forecasts 1.38 crore jobs as consumer electronics, retail and manufacturing drive demand
MUMBAI: India’s job market could be ready to shift into a higher gear in 2027, with employers expected to loosen the brakes on recruitment after a year of cautious expansion. White-collar job opportunities are projected to reach 1.38 crore, with hiring growth forecast at 8.16 per cent, according to the latest foundit Insights Tracker.
The projection marks a considerable improvement on the 3.30 per cent year-on-year growth recorded in 2026, when companies remained selective about adding to their workforces. While technology, healthcare, real estate and travel and tourism supported recruitment during the year, the next phase of growth is expected to spread across a wider range of industries, including consumer electronics, retail, manufacturing, banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI), and logistics.
“2026 has been a year of measured hiring. Employers expanded their teams thoughtfully and placed a premium on experienced professionals,” said foundit CEO Tarun Sinha.
He added that the expected pickup in 2027 could extend opportunities to more cities, sectors and early-career professionals, indicating a broader recovery rather than growth concentrated in a handful of industries.
The sectoral picture in 2026 was uneven. Non-profit organisations recorded the highest hiring growth at 19.44 per cent, followed by real estate at 16.09 per cent, travel and tourism at 13.76 per cent, and healthcare and pharmaceuticals at 12.34 per cent.
Some industries, however, continued to face pressure. BFSI hiring declined by 5 per cent, while logistics and transportation recorded a 2.52 per cent fall.
The outlook for 2027 points to a change in momentum. Consumer electronics is expected to lead sectoral hiring growth at 14.25 per cent, followed by retail at 13.99 per cent and manufacturing at 12.02 per cent.
BFSI and logistics and transportation are also projected to return to positive territory, with hiring growth of 10.03 per cent and 10.15 per cent, respectively. The projected turnaround in these sectors suggests that recruitment demand could broaden beyond the industries that supported hiring through 2026.
Technology-related roles continued to stand out in 2026, even as the wider IT industry experienced a slowdown. IT roles recorded the strongest occupational hiring growth at 20.28 per cent, while the IT software and services sector registered a 1.66 per cent decline.
The difference highlights how demand for technology professionals is not necessarily tied to recruitment by IT companies alone. Businesses across industries continue to require specialised digital capabilities.
Senior management roles recorded 8.11 per cent growth in 2026, while marketing and communications positions increased by 7.21 per cent.
For 2027, IT hiring is projected to grow by 10.30 per cent. HR and administration roles are expected to record 8.93 per cent growth, followed by senior management positions at 8.56 per cent.
The geographical distribution of recruitment is also expected to change. Hyderabad led city-wise hiring growth in 2026 at 8.51 per cent, followed by Bengaluru at 6.71 per cent, Mumbai at 6.15 per cent and Kochi at 5.57 per cent.
Not all major employment centres shared that momentum. Hiring declined by 11.19 per cent in Chandigarh and 10.03 per cent in Kolkata, while Delhi-NCR recorded a 3.40 per cent fall.
The 2027 projections put Coimbatore at the top of the city-wise growth chart, with hiring expected to rise by 12.52 per cent. This would mark a turnaround from the city’s 1.86 per cent decline in 2026.
Bengaluru is projected to record 11.29 per cent growth, followed by Hyderabad at 10.33 per cent. Delhi-NCR is also expected to return to positive territory, with hiring forecast to increase by 6.79 per cent.
The projections suggest that recruitment growth could become more geographically distributed, giving employers and jobseekers opportunities beyond the country’s established employment hubs.
Experience remained an important factor in recruitment decisions during 2026. Professionals with seven to 10 years of experience recorded the strongest hiring growth among experience categories at 8.63 per cent, while those with 11 to 15 years of experience saw demand rise by 5.54 per cent.
Entry-level hiring was considerably slower. Recruitment for professionals with zero to three years of experience grew by just 0.69 per cent, while the four-to-six-year category recorded a 0.35 per cent decline.
The 2027 outlook points to some improvement for younger professionals, with entry-level hiring projected to grow by 4.64 per cent. Demand for professionals with seven to 10 years of experience is expected to increase by 7.51 per cent.
The seven-to-10-year experience bracket is also forecast to account for 21 per cent of overall hiring demand in 2027, underlining the continued importance of mid-career talent as companies look for professionals who can contribute with limited ramp-up time.
Beyond the number of vacancies, employers are expected to place greater emphasis on productivity, operational efficiency and measurable business outcomes. Hiring linked to these priorities is projected to increase by 15 to 20 per cent.
Demand is also expected to rise for specialised capabilities in areas such as risk, compliance and cybersecurity. The supplied report details do not specify a corresponding growth percentage for these skills.
At the same time, companies are likely to look increasingly towards reskilling existing employees and moving talent internally to fill business requirements. Such initiatives could account for 20 to 30 per cent of positions filled, according to the outlook.
Taken together, the projections point to a job market moving beyond the cautious recruitment patterns of 2026. Technology skills and experienced professionals are expected to remain important, but stronger demand across consumer-facing industries, manufacturing, BFSI and logistics could widen the range of opportunities.
The bigger test for 2027 will be whether the projected recovery translates into more vacancies across experience levels and locations, particularly for early-career candidates who saw limited hiring momentum in the previous year.

global-economics-0472bec9c7.headline: US blacklists Megaspeed, targeting firm central to Nvidia crisis
global-economics-0472bec9c7.source: Business News Today: Latest Business News, Finance News
global-economics-0472bec9c7.fulltext:
Updated - November 24, 2026  at 09:44 AM.
The Trump administration put Megaspeed International on a US trade blacklist that bars it from buying advanced artificial intelligence chips, targeting a Singapore-based firm at the heart of the scandal that briefly cost Jensen Huang his job as Nvidia Corp. chief executive officer.
In a filing Monday, the Commerce Department moved to formally add Megaspeed to its so-called entity list, a designation that would effectively prohibit the company from buying AI chips and other advanced technology without a US government license. The listing named six other entities in Singapore, Thailand and Malaysia, citing US concerns that their activities could pose a threat to US national security.
“These additions are being made because of the significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized end uses or end users,” the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, said in the filing.
Other ventures listed by Commerce included Singapore-based Apex Enterprise Solutions, along with a Malaysia subsidiary of Megaspeed called Speedmatrix.
The announcement was released before the start of normal business hours in Asia. Megaspeed has previously denied wrongdoing and said that it complies with all applicable US and local laws governing shipments of advanced technology.
Commerce posted its decision hours after Nvidia’s board brought Huang back as CEO in a stunning reversal of his ouster from the company less than two weeks ago. Huang had resigned after admitting to multiple extramarital affairs, including with a woman named Alice Huang who had been a top Megaspeed executive and was suspected by the US of spying for China.
Jensen Huang’s return to the top job at Nvidia came after President Donald Trump intervened with the chipmaker’s board, offering his assurances that there would be no threat to national security in bringing the ousted CEO back to the company he had co-founded more than three decades ago. Trump had been open about his desire to see Huang return as Nvidia chief, saying publicly that he saw it as critical to US economic security.
Revelations earlier this month about Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang put a fresh spotlight on allegations that Megaspeed may have been smuggling Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips into China. The episode spurred questions about whether Commerce had been rigorously enforcing US export controls designed to keep sensitive technology from falling into adversaries’ hands.
Once the spinoff of a Chinese gaming enterprise called 7Road, Megaspeed rose to prominence amid the AI boom, but for more than a year, the US government has been investigating both its ownership structure and whether it has smuggled Nvidia chips into China. The Justice Department has also been probing Jensen Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, who had been in contact with China’s top spy agency for more than a year while she was romantically involved with the Nvidia CEO, according to New York Times reporting.
Megaspeed has said that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025. She is now in China with the knowledge of the government in Beijing, Bloomberg has reported.
In joint statement published last week, the Justice and Commerce Departments provided a rare update on their investigations into potential export control violations by Megaspeed. The agencies said the US inquiry began in 2024 and that in May 2025, Commerce officials had requested Megaspeed sales records from Nvidia.
In June last year, Nvidia placed Megaspeed on its so-called no sell list, the agencies said, but the Bureau of Industry and Security which is responsible for enforcing rules that restrict chip sales to China never placed the firm on its own blacklist. Around the same time, BIS said its agents conducted an end-use check of Megaspeed and interviewed Alice Huang, who is now in China.
Commerce officials had come under intensifying pressure to list Megaspeed by US lawmakers, who seized on the turmoil at Nvidia to press for answers about enforcement of export restrictions. Last week, Republican Senator Pete Ricketts proposed legislation that would have forced Commerce to decide within 30 days whether to blacklist Megaspeed and impose interim restrictions in the meantime.
Adding to the tension, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had publicly blamed Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in recent weeks for failing to put Megaspeed on the entity list. “Many other departments were pushing for this, and Commerce had the pen,” Bessent said on CNBC the day after Huang’s resignation.
Yet before departing last week for a trip to Asia, where he would take part in a series of regional summits, Trump backed Lutnick publicly, saying that he understood both sides of the issue and that his Commerce Secretary was simply being careful not to upset China.
Enthusiasm for the entity listing faded among some advocates of a tougher stance toward China, including Chris McGuire, a former National Security Council official, who questioned whether it was written in a way that would allow the US to block the sale of AI chips to Megaspeed at all.
The interim rule published Monday differed from previous entity listings targeting AI chip purchases of blacklisted firms because it left out a footnote that’s often present to make it clear that foreign-produced items are included in export bans so long as they contain US technology. That led McGuire to question whether the measure has enough authority to block the listed firms from purchasing AI chips, an interpretation that BIS officials rejected.
“It is now unlawful to export any advanced SI chips to Megaspeed, even if the chips are produced outside the United States,” BIS spokesperson Thomas Wackman said in a statement, using Trump’s preferred term of super intelligence to refer to AI.
A Commerce official added that there’s no need for BIS to include a provision giving the US extraterritorial authority for the rule to have an impact, since existing regulations already carry that authority for advanced computing, which puts all AI chips shipped abroad under BIS jurisdiction.
Megaspeed’s blacklisting marked the latest in a series of recent moves by the administration to tighten up its handling of export controls in the wake of the Nvidia scandal. Last week, the Commerce Department unveiled a rule designed to limit the ability of Chinese firms to access Nvidia’s AI chips in data centers located outside China.
The measure requires data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to obtain a US government license before exporting advanced AI chips from Nvidia and other American manufacturers to customers in those countries.
The Commerce Department said that the rule was “written by and at the direction” of the Treasury Department and the National Security Council, suggesting that pressure from officials outside Commerce played a significant role in its release. The licenses are subject to approval on a case-by-case basis.
Propelled by the Nvidia scandal, Republican and Democratic lawmakers are rallying behind legislation that would curtail China’s access to AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment that may win passage within weeks.
Bipartisan export-control bills including the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act are on course to be attached to year-end defense legislation, backed by top AI developers including OpenAI.
